title: Harnessing gasotransmitters for orthopaedic infection therapy: Mechanisms and advanced delivery platforms
abstract: Orthopaedic infections are increasingly prevalent in the aging population, posing a significant clinical and economic burden. Despite progress in antimicrobial therapies, challenges such as antibiotic resistance and superbug emergence persist. Gas therapy has emerged as a promising strategy for managing orthopaedic infections. Classical gasotransmitters-including nitric oxide (NO), carbon monoxide (CO), and hydrogen sulfide (HS)-exhibit antibacterial and immunomodulatory effects at controlled concentrations, though improper dosing may induce adverse effects. This review critically examines the dual mechanisms through which gasotransmitters combat infection while promoting orthopaedic regeneration. We also survey advanced delivery platforms-such as smart scaffolds, nano-reservoirs, and on-demand release systems-engineered for targeted gasotransmitter delivery to infected bone tissue. Finally, we discuss current limitations and future prospects, aiming to inspire novel biomaterial designs for targeted therapeutic delivery and to advance gas therapy as a viable option for orthopaedic infection treatment.

title: Bioprinted core-shell living material platform for spatially controlled encapsulation of Bacillus subtilis and sustained metabolite exchange
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) represents an escalating global health crisis, demanding alternative strategies to reduce resistant pathogen burden across environments. Microbe-based biocontrol is promising, yet effectively deploying it in practical settings remains challenging. In this study, we present a 3D bioprinted core-shell construct featuring a polyethylene glycol diacrylate (PEGDA) shell with tunable nanoscale porosity, encapsulating germinable spores of the biocontrol agentTH035. This configuration supports long-term spore viability while providing protection from common environmental stressors including UV-C irradiation, ethanol exposure, and desiccation over 4 weeks. The nanoporous PEGDA shell enables effective bacterial confinement while facilitating sufficient metabolite exchange forgermination and growth, as well as suppression of methicillin-resistant(MRSA) growth by approximately one order of magnitude. This approach demonstrates the feasibility of embeddingspores within engineered scaffolds for extended competitive functionality. The versatility and scalability of digital light processing (DLP) based bioprinting offers significant potential for tailored designs and high-throughput manufacturing. This proof-of-concept platform may find future applications in areas such as biomedical packaging, environmental sanitation, and built environment surface coatings, particularly in settings where intermittent moisture or nutrient availability can support spore germination and biocontrol activity.

title: Artificial intelligence catalyzes antimicrobial peptide design
abstract: With broad-spectrum, low resistance, and multifunctional properties, antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are promising therapeutic agents against drug-resistant pathogens, yet their discovery and optimization still remain challenging due to the complexity of sequence-function associations. Artificial intelligence (AI), through the construction of comprehensive data-driven models that assisted with miscellaneous learning strategies, enables de novo peptide design by learning latent representations inherent in peptide sequences as well as their biological properties to ensure physically plausible and biologically relevant predictions. Consequently, this paradigm enhances the likelihood of designing peptide candidates with significantly improved therapeutic potential, reducing resource-intensive trial-and-error processes and revealing the transformative impact of computational innovation in advancing next-generation therapeutics. Here, we provide a snapshot of this field and survey two modes of AI-driven technologies for AMP design, one concentrated on identifying whether current data possess antimicrobial activity (identification-oriented) and the other on generating AMP candidates with potential therapeutic properties (generation-oriented). We also highlight the challenges and limitations that still hinder AMP development even accelerated by AI, as well as the foreseeable prospects, from finer-grained explorations to model-driven data enrichment and model enhancement.

title: Antifungal mechanisms of volatile organic compounds and lactic acid produced by Lactiplantibacillus pentosus and their biocontrol application in fresh corn against Fusarium graminearum
abstract: Fusarium graminearum causes cereal spoilage and mycotoxin production. Currently, biocontrol microorganisms have emerged as a safe and promising strategy to manage the contamination of toxin-producing fungi in cereal grains. The primary objective was to elucidate the antifungal mechanism of an isolated strain of Lactiplantibacillus pentosus Q11 against F. graminearum and to evaluate the preservative effects of its cell-free supernatant (CFS) in fresh sweet corn. In vitro antifungal assays of L. pentosus Q11 showed strong antagonistic activity against F. graminearum, Aspergillus flavus, and Penicillium expansum, as well as the ability to reduce zearalenone. Moreover, whole-genome analysis revealed no genes related to virulence and antimicrobial resistance, and no hemolytic activity was observed, which suggested the potential safety of strain Q11. Moreover, the CFS of L. pentosus Q11 effectively inhibited the mycelial growth of F. graminearum, disrupted hyphal integrity, and induced fungal cell death. Moreover, 3 organic acids and 38 volatile compounds in the CFS of Q11 strain were identified by SPME-GC-MS and HPLC, in which 2-nonanone, 2-methylpyrazine, lactic acid, acetic acid were predominant compounds. The CFS and lactic acid combined with 2-nonanone severely damaged hyphae of F. graminearum, by disrupting cell membrane and wall, leading to leakage of intracellular substances, showing a synergistic antifungal effect of the two vital compounds. Subsequently, the treatments of CFS and combined agents significantly decreased 88.05% - 89.52% of fungal populations, and AFBand DON mycotoxin accumulation in fresh sweet corn after 12 days of storage compared to the control. The malondialdehyde content in the treated corn was decreased by 29.25% - 31.50%, consistent with the higher activities of POD and APX, thereby preserving their sensory attributes and nutritional quality. Metabolomic analysis revealed that L-glutamate, γ-glutamylcysteine, and oxidized glutathione were significantly downregulated in the glutathione metabolism pathway in the treated corn, indicating that CFS containing lactic acid and 2-nonanone could repress fungal growth and alleviate oxidative stress in fresh sweet corn. Overall, these findings demonstrate that L. pentosus Q11 with synergistic volatile organic compounds and lactic acid is a promising biocontrol agent in preserving fresh sweet corn.

abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is escalating in East Africa through close human-animal-environment interactions. Extended-spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBL) and carbapenemase-producingare clinically critical pathogens, yet local evidence is limited. This scoping review synthesizes evidence on ESBL and carbapenemase-producingin East Africa to inform One Health AMR control strategies. Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, PubMed and Scopus were searched, identifying 279 records published between 2015 and 2025. After removing duplicates and screening, 185 articles were assessed for eligibility; 154 studies spanning human, animal and environmental sources met the inclusion criteria. Two reviewers independently extracted epidemiological, microbiological and molecular data in Covidence, including resistance genes and transmission evidence. The 154 included studies spanned 11 East African countries, led by Ethiopia ( = 55), Tanzania ( = 39) and Uganda ( = 22). Most studies (85.7%) were cross-sectional and human-focused (68.2%), with only 19 (12.3%) using a multi-sector One Health design. Overall, 21,554isolates were recovered from 74,700 samples. ESBL prevalence was reported in 117 studies (76.0%, median 46.8%) and carbapenemase prevalence in 65 (42.2%, median 3.3%), representing heterogeneous study-level estimates.predominated (89.9%), led by(26.1%); reported carbapenemase genes included,,andWhole-genome sequencing in 30 studies (19.5%) identified high-risk clones ST131, ST10, ST38 and ST410, though animal, food-chain and environmental sectors remained underrepresented. This review maps the current evidence on landscape for ESBL/carbapenemase- producingin East Africa, highlighting gaps in surveillance that are largely due to heterogeneity of available genomics data and limited longitudinal data within the "One Health" sectors. We recommend scaling up genomic capacity and standardized longitudinal surveillance to better understand national and regional AMR transmission and MDRinfections.

title: DNA augmentations for semi-supervised learning in genomic sequence classification
abstract: Semi-supervised learning (SSL) is a natural fit for genomics, where unlabeled sequences are abundant but high-quality labels are scarce due to costly curation. However, most SSL pipelines rely on generic perturbations that are not tailored to biological constraints, and it remains unclear which augmentation designs yield reliable gains for DNA sequence classification. In this application note, we present an empirical study of genome-aware weak-strong augmentation recipes for pseudo-label-based SSL, focusing on FixMatch and FlexMatch with a GROVER DNA language model backbone. Across two classification benchmarks-antimicrobial resistance (AMR) drug-class prediction from AMR gene sequences and multi-class oncovirus family classification from simulated 150 bp tumor-like reads-we systematically evaluate 25 weak/strong augmentation pairs constructed from biologically motivated operators, including reverse-complement, codon-level back-translation, mild masking/substitution (NN), high-rate substitution, and length-preserving insertion-deletion (indel). We find consistent trends: (i) moderate, sequence-preserving perturbations yield the best accuracy-stability trade-off, (ii) excessive masking or aggressive mutation increases variance and degrades performance, and (iii) short-segment masking (NN) for weak augmentation followed by an indel rate (around 5%) for strong augmentation emerge as a robust strategy to learn from unlabeled genomic data. We release implementations and recommended defaults to facilitate reproducible SSL for genomic sequence modeling under limited-label regimes.

title: Synergistic functions of copper-based nanomaterials modified granular activated carbon: antibacterial activity, antibiotics adsorption, and impact of preceding chlorination on antibiotic resistance genes removal in tertiary treated hospital effluents
abstract: The synergistic efficacy and mechanisms of antibacterial activity and adsorption of antibiotics/intermediates using copper-based nanomaterials modified granular activated carbon (GAC) were evaluated, including the impact of preceding chlorination on the reduction of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) and antibiotic-resistant bacteria (ARB) in effluents treated by fixed-bed column. Copper-based MOFs coated on GACs (GAC-CuBDC and GAC-CuNHBDC) exhibited higher antibacterial efficacy than the functionalized GACs (-COOH and -NH) and copper oxide (CuO and CuO)-coated GACs, which 100% eliminated both Gram-negativeand Gram-positivebacteria (5.5 and 5.1 log reduction, respectively). Notably, GAC-CuBDC can inhibit the growth of total bacteria and presumptivein the matrix of hospital effluents to non-detectable levels; however, interference from dissolved organic matter in the effluents can reduce antibacterial efficacy, requiring an increased solid-to-liquid ratio from 4 to 8 g/L to achieve 100% inhibition. Hydrophilic GAC-CuBDC exhibited high performance in adsorbing intermediates derived from penicillin G, ampicillin, ceftazidime, and ciprofloxacin. The intermediates found in chlorinated effluent could be more easily eliminated by functionalized GACs than those in non-chlorinated effluent. The adsorption capacities of penicillin G, ceftazidime, and ciprofloxacin onto GAC-CuBDC were comparable to those of pristine GAC, whereas ampicillin showed a two-fold higher adsorption on GAC-CuBDC than on pristine GAC. Adsorption mechanisms of antibiotics onto GAC-CuBDC may include hydrogen bonding and π-π interactions (involving -NH and nitroaromatic ring of the antibiotic) with the acidic functional groups of GAC, combined with hydrogen bonding at the terminal -OH groups of the CuBDC copper nodes. Passage through the fixed-bed column of GAC-CuBDC could reduce the intracellular ARGs and ARB from hospital effluents. However, the coexistence of chlorination may promote the growth ofand interfere with the reduction of some ARGs and ARB after tertiary treatment by the GAC-CuBDC column. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s40201-026-01007-w.

Dietary licorice improves carcass yield, hepatocellular protection, gut health, oxidative status, and cecal bacterial balance in broiler chickens
abstract: Over the past decade, phytotherapy such as licorice has attracted research as an alternative to antibiotic growth promoters in broiler production, driven by rising concerns over antimicrobial resistance. However, the consistency of its effects across productive, physiological, and health outcomes remains inconsistent. This meta-analysis quantitatively synthesized published experimental evidence on the effects of dietary licorice on growth performance, carcass yield, blood indices, visceral organs, oxidative status, intestinal morphology, and cecal bacterial balance in broiler chickens. A systematic literature search identified studies published between 2010 and 2025, and effect sizes were computed (Hedges'; 95% confidence interval). Pooled estimates were derived under the random-effects model using the restricted maximum likelihood estimator, with between-study heterogeneity characterized bythe-statistic. Univariable mixed-effects meta-regression was conducted to identify study-level moderators of treatment response, and publication bias was assessed using a funnel plot and the Rosenberg fail-safe N criterion. Dietary licorice did not affect feed intake or the feed conversion ratio, but it did increase body weight gain (BWG; SMD = 0.289; = 0.002), breast, thigh, gizzard, and bursa weights ( < 0.05). Gut integrity also improved with the villus height/crypt depth ratio (SMD = 0.931; = 0.041), andspp. counts (SMD = 0.266; = 0.003) increased, whilepopulations were suppressed (SMD = -1.737; < 0.001). Overall, the findings support that licorice enhances body weight gain, with route, duration, sex, and strain moderating efficacy.

Staphylococcus aureus in bovine intramammary infections: A global systematic review and meta-analysis of prevalence and antimicrobial resistance patterns
abstract: ()is a globally pervasive and economically significant pathogen in bovine intramammary infections (IMIs) and is responsible for both clinical and subclinical mastitis. This study systematically investigated the global epidemiology offrom bovine IMIs, addressing antimicrobial resistance (AMR) amongthrough a meta-analysis. A total of 143 studies published between 2000 and 2025 were identified through comprehensive searches, which were based on predefined inclusion criteria. The data were systematically extracted, and the statistical analyses were performed in R (v4.5.2). The meta-analysis included 143 studies (145,457 samples), with a pooledprevalence of 24.78% and high heterogeneity (I = 99.51%). Subgroup analyses demonstrated significant heterogeneity in prevalence by study design, publication year, and region, with greater heterogeneity in cross-sectional studies (I>95%, < 0.001). Meta-regression identified sample size as a significant source of heterogeneity (β = -0.00002, = 0.02; R = 3.41%). The highest prevalence was reported in Cameroon (67%), Sri Lanka (64.3%), Indonesia (57%), and India (44%), with the lowest prevalence reported in Poland (0.7%), Taiwan (2.0%), Australia (5.5%), and New Zealand (5.3%). AMR was highest for doxycycline (70.7%), penicillin (65.2%), and ampicillin (62.8%); moderate to oxacillin (44.6%) and vancomycin (40.2%); and lowest for gentamicin (27.5%) and amikacin (18.3%). is highly prevalent in bovine IMIs worldwide, with marked regional heterogeneity and substantial resistance to commonly used antimicrobials, emphasizing the urgent need for targeted surveillance, prudent antimicrobial use, and improved mastitis control strategies at the global and regional levels.

N-acetylcysteine as an adjunct to antibiotics against bacterial biofilms: A systematic review of in vitro evidence
abstract: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is investigated as an antibiotic adjunct, but acidity, formulation and experimental context complicate interpretation. We evaluated comparative in-vitro evidence while distinguishing biofilm prevention, established-biofilm treatment and resistance evolution. MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Scopus and Web of Science were searched through August 2026, with supplementary searching. Extraction distinguished NAC preparation and exposure pH, medium, hydrodynamics, NAC-alone controls, treatment intent and interaction methodology. Results were synthesized by experimental context, regimen, phase and endpoint without pooling or whole-study efficacy voting. Fifty-five studies were included: 7 evaluated combination exposure during formation only, 37 after establishment only, 9 both, and 2 resistance evolution. NAC-alone arms were documented in 39 studies, partial or formulation-specific in 9, and not identified in 7. Only two studies included a continuous-flow model. Selected combinations improved biofilm-associated outcomes, but intrinsic-acidic and neutralized preparations, biomass and viability endpoints, and planktonic versus biofilm interaction tests were not interchangeable. Liposomal and catheter-lock findings differed by dose matching, isolate and control set. Polymyxin findings varied with organism, resistance background, medium and exposure; rifampicin-alone and rifampicin-containing multidrug comparators addressed different questions. NAC is a context-dependent experimental adjunct, not an established class-wide antibiotic potentiator. The evidence does not support clinical antibiotic dose reduction or routine NAC combination therapy. Translation requires controlled final exposure pH, matched monotherapy and formulation controls, clinically relevant background regimens, viable-burden and regrowth outcomes, and resistance monitoring.

Combating antimicrobial resistance through multimodal data via artificial intelligence
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a critical global health challenge, leading to substantial mortality and economic losses without science-based interventions. Conventional approaches to combating AMR have important limitations in addressing this escalating threat. Recent advances in AI, including deep learning, large language models, and protein language models, provide new opportunities to integrate multimodal data for AMR research. However, evidence remains uneven, with many approaches limited to computational benchmarking rather than real-world validation. Here, we critically review AI applications in AMR, focusing on rapid diagnosis, therapeutic discovery, and clinical decision support. AI-based diagnostic models can identify resistant pathogens and predict resistance profiles, but most lack prospective clinical evaluation. AI-assisted drug discovery and alternative therapies have generated promising candidates, although most remain at computational, in vitro, or early preclinical stages. Large language models may support decision-making, but their clinical use remains preliminary. Successful translation of AI into clinical and One Health practice will require representative datasets, independent validation, prospective evaluation, and robust governance.

abstract: Mastitis is a multifactorial disease with major consequences for production, animal welfare, and public health, yet it remains less studied in goats than in cows. Moreover, reports of antimicrobial resistance among bacteria isolated from mastitic goats are scarce. In Ethiopia, treatment decisions for mastitis largely rely on empirical clinical experience rather than routine antimicrobial susceptibility testing. To address this gap, a cross-sectional study was conducted from November to December 2024 in Waghimra, Amhara, Ethiopia, to identify the major bacterial causes of mastitis and to evaluate their antimicrobial susceptibility patterns. Bacterial isolation, identification, and antimicrobial susceptibility testing followed standard protocols, and statistical analyses were performed using Stata 17 and WHONET software. Allisolates were resistant to ampicillin (37/37; 100%) and showed considerable resistance to tetracycline (16/37; 43.24%), but remained highly susceptible to kanamycin (36/37; 97.30%), chloramphenicol, and gentamicin (35/37; 94.59% each).andspp. were highly susceptible to most antimicrobials tested, except ampicillin. Multidrug resistance was detected in 13.46% (7 out of 52) of isolates, occurring exclusively amongspp. Subclinical mastitis, mainly caused byspp., was highly prevalent in the study area, showing complete ampicillin resistance and considerable tetracycline resistance. Strengthening One Health Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance in Bangladesh: Insights from the Fleming fund country grant
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is an escalating global public health concern, with particularly severe implications for low and middle-income countries such as Bangladesh. In Bangladesh context, fragmented surveillance systems and the extensive use of antimicrobials across human, animal, and aquaculture sectors contribute to the rapid emergence and spread of resistance. Strengthening integrated surveillance through a One Health approach is therefore crucial to support effective policy development and response strategies. This review outlines the policy, implementation, and key outcomes of the Fleming Fund Country Grant in Bangladesh between 2020 and 2025. It draws upon multiple data sources, including programme reports, routine AMR surveillance data, laboratory capacity-building initiatives, and stakeholder engagement activities across human, animal, aquaculture, and environmental sectors. Through this initiative, a coordinated national AMR surveillance network was established, comprising 20 laboratories across multiple sectors, including three designated national reference laboratories. The initiative strengthened surveillance through the introduction of standardized protocols and SOPs, improved diagnostic capacity, skilled workforce, and implementation of laboratory quality assurance systems, including EQA and NEQA. These measures enhanced the accuracy, consistency, and reliability of AMR surveillance data. In addition, the establishment of a national AMR data integration platform facilitated real time data sharing and evidence-based decision-making. A total of 208,346 bacterial isolates were analyzed, with AST results reported to the AMR dashboard across the human, and animal, health sectors. Overall, the Fleming Fund programme has made a substantial contribution to strengthening integrated AMR surveillance in Bangladesh by operationalizing a One Health framework. Continued political commitment, increased domestic investment, and the institutionalization of surveillance systems will be essential to sustain these gains and ensure long-term resilience against AMR.

Microfluidic-assembled curcumin ionizable lipid nanoparticles enhance aqueous delivery and antibiofilm activity against Staphylococcus aureus
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance and biofilm-associated infections demand novel therapeutic strategies. Curcumin is a natural polyphenol with broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity; however, its clinical utility is fundamentally constrained by negligible aqueous solubility and limited biofilm penetration. Here, we used microfluidic assembly to prepare curcumin-loaded ionizable lipid nanoparticles (Cur@LNP) with three clinically established ionizable lipids (SM-102, MC-3, and ALC-0315). The resulting formulations were uniform, with hydrodynamic diameters of approximately 90 nm and polydispersity indices near 0.1. Relative to free curcumin in DMSO, Cur@LNP lowered the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) 8-fold and the minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) 16-fold against planktonic, and markedly reduced viable biofilm-resident cells at matched concentrations. Scanning electron microscopy showed that Cur@LNP treatment remodeled mature biofilms into irregular, debris-rich aggregates with reduced extracellular matrix coverage. Notably, antimicrobial performance was indistinguishable across the three structurally distinct ionizable lipids at every concentration tested. Within this in vitro, single-strain system, the antibiofilm effect is therefore dominated by the cargo (curcumin) rather than by ionizable-lipid chemistry, and it is most likely attributed to enhanced aqueous solubilization of curcumin rather than to engagement of the lipid headgroup with the biofilm matrix. These results position microfluidic-assembled ionizable LNPs as a reproducible, scalable solubilization platform for poorly water-soluble natural antimicrobials.

title: Metagenomic analysis of commensal small mammal samples from an international cargo shipping area, Bangkok Port, reveals potential zoonotic pathogens and implications for One Health surveillance
abstract: Commensal small mammals, such as rats and shrews, are recognized reservoirs for numerous zoonotic pathogens; however, their role in pathogen circulation at transport hubs remains underexplored. This study employs shotgun metagenomic sequencing to characterize microbial communities and assess zoonotic potential in tissue samples from commensal small mammals captured at Bangkok Port, an international cargo shipping hub in Thailand between June and August 2025. Following host read depletion, taxonomic profiling was performed to identify bacterial taxa of public health relevance, including sequences assigned tospp.,,, and. The virulence factor and antibiotic resistance gene profiles revealed that some of these pathogens have pathogenic potential and are related to drug-resistant bacteria. In addition,was identified as a shared taxon among rats, shrews, and their associated fleas. The findings support the ecological roles of mammalian hosts and their ectoparasites as reservoirs for pathogens of public health concern. These results emphasize the need to strengthen surveillance programs for commensal small mammals to monitor and mitigate the spread of transboundary pathogens at international maritime gateways.

Wild boar as a sentinel species for ecosystem health surveillance: A review
abstract: Sentinel surveillance uses selected species that are widely distributed, easily sampled, and exposed to multiple health threats as indicators of ecosystem health. The Eurasian wild boar () is a broadly distributed game species that meets these conditions. We conducted a systematic review to assess the suitability of the wild boar as a sentinel or indicator species for monitoring health hazards relevant to ecosystem health, focusing on the hazards monitored, methods, justification for use, perceived performance, limitations, and proposed improvements. We identified 86 studies explicitly framing the wild boar as a sentinel species, covering a wide range of hazards, including 30 pathogens, 44 environmental contaminants, two biological toxins and 13 antimicrobial resistance (AMR) indicators. It was used to monitor pathogens (57%), environmental contaminants (31.4%), AMR (12.8%), and biological toxins (3.5%). Research effort was concentrated in Europe (84.9%) and relied mostly on hunted animals (90.7%). Wild boar were frequently selected as sentinels due to their previous use as indicators of ecosystem health in the literature, omnivorous diet, wide distribution, and accessibility as game species. However, hunting-based sampling may introduce biases, while post-mortem conditions and ecological variability may affect results. Despite this, 74.4% of studies supported their use as sentinels, particularly for pathogens and environmental contaminants. In contrast, their perceived suitability for AMR was more variable, and no quality assessment was available for biological toxins. Overall, wild boar sentinel surveillance is considered logistically efficient and valuable for monitoring ecosystem health hazards. However, its effectiveness is context-dependent and influenced by methodological and ecological limitations. Improving surveillance design through systematic sampling, alternative sample sources (e.g., found-dead animals or non-invasive methods), integration of multi-species data, and inclusion of covariates could enhance the reliability of findings within a One Health framework.

title: Global spread of carbapenem-resistant Providencia driven by high-risk lineages and plasmid co-evolution
abstract: Carbapenem-resistant(CRP) is a formidable opportunistic pathogen with extensive drug resistance, posing an increasing threat to human, animal, and environmental health. However, its global genomic epidemiology and resistome-plasmidome co-evolution within a One Health context remain poorly understood. Here, we conducted a comprehensive population genomic and plasmid analysis of 1197 CRP isolates from 35 countries spanning 2012-2025. We reclassified the CRP population into ninespecies, identifyingandas established epidemic species alongside the rapid emergence ofand. We pinpointed 2019 as a critical inflection point, marking the transition from endemic stability to rapid global epidemic expansion (80.8% isolates in 2019-2025). Ten intercontinentally disseminated high-risk sequence types (e.g., ST46, ST79), each with strict species-ST specificity, were responsible for global spread. Thegene (62.4% prevalence) was the predominant carbapenem gene, exhibiting strong geographic and species specificity and mutual exclusion with other major carbapenem genes. Plasmids encoded approximately 80% of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes, with 78.0% of these plasmids belonging to 75 stable clusters. These clusters evolved a dual specialist-generalist strategy, with the broad-host-range cluster 72 mediating interspecies AMR transmission and cluster 7 acting as a super-vector carrying six carbapenem genes. Importantly, CRP circulated across interconnected human, animal, and environmental reservoirs, with distinct host-associated species distributions suggesting ecological niche adaptation and potential cross-host dissemination of resistance determinants. These findings demonstrate that the global expansion of CRP is driven by the combined evolution of high-risk clones and mobile genetic elements across interconnected ecological sectors, underscoring the need for integrated One Health surveillance and coordinated interventions spanning clinical, veterinary, agricultural, and environmental settings.

abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has intensified in recent years, raising concerns about the potential impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on AMR dynamics. However, the influence of pandemic on the enviromental occurrence and dissemination of antibiotic-resistant genes (ARGs) remains under investigation. Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) provides an integrated view of community-level AMR dynamics, yet long-term assessments spanning the pandemic period remain limited. This study investigated the occurrence, temporal patterns, and seasonal behavior of two clinically relevant carbapenemase genes,and, in raw wastewater from the Attica region over a five-year period (July 2021-September 2025). A sensitive and specific 3-plex qPCR assay was developed and analytically validated for the simultaneous quantification of,, and 16S rRNA, the latter serving as a stable bacterial load indicator. Across the monitoring period,was consistently detected, showing a steady increase and reaching its highest concentrations in 2023, whileexhibited intermittent but pronounced surges, particularly in 2023. Comparison with community SARS-CoV-2 viral loads suggest temporal association with AMR signatures in wastewater. Seasonal analysis showed non-uniform patterns, with atypical warm-season peaks of both ARGs in 2023-2024 and a return to classical autumn-winter peaks in 2025, suggesting a gradual restoration of pre-pandemic seasonality. To our knowledge, this is among the first long-term WBE studies to characterize post-COVID-19 shifts in ARG occurrence and seasonality. The results demonstrate that the pandemic period was associated with elevated and fluctuating ARG levels in the urban wastewater system, emphasizing the need for sustained AMR monitoring. These findings address critical knowledge gaps in environmental AMR surveillance and support the integration of WBE into public health strategies aimed at mitigating AMR dissemination.

title: Prevalence of antimicrobial-resistant Escherichia coli as an indicator bacterium in livestock and companion animals in Mongolia
Genomic epidemiology to investigate the origins and zoonotic implications of antibiotic-resistant Escherichia coli on beef and lamb meat sold by independent butchers in Wales
abstract: Many studies have identified antibiotic resistant (ABR)on meat. Appropriate hand hygiene and cooking practices should minimize the risk of gastrointestinal colonisation with ABRfound on meat, and the subsequent chance of causing resistant opportunistic extraintestinal infection. There are large gaps in our understanding of the prevalence, origins and zoonotic potential of ABRfound on meat, however, and particularly for meat reared in extensive farming systems. Wales is a devolved nation within the United Kingdom having large populations of extensively-reared sheep and beef cattle. To help address knowledge gaps around ABRon extensively reared meat, therefore, beef mince and lamb loin/leg steaks/chops were purchased from 50 (beef) and 46 (lamb) independent butchers across Wales. Following enrichment culture, 200 g meat samples were found to be positive forresistant to amoxicillin (31% positivity), streptomycin (28%), spectinomycin (29%), amoxicillin-clavulanate (11%), 3rd generation cephalosporins (2%) and fluoroquinolones (5%). Phylogenetic analysis confirmed that Welsh lamb meat ABRisolates ( = 78) are more closely related to those found in faecal samples collected around sheep ( = 352) than around beef cattle ( = 361) on Welsh farms. This suggests that faecal contamination at or around slaughter is their primary origin. We found no closely related meat/infection clones (<20 SNPs distant and the same antibiotic resistance genes) when comparing ABRfrom Welsh meat ( = 91) and those causing extraintestinal infections in people ( = 2387) in an English region bordering Wales. We conclude, therefore, that the wider zoonotic implications of finding ABRon beef and lamb meat sold at independent butchers in Wales are small, though a more geographically and temporarily contemporaneous survey is warranted to address this further.

title: Genomic insights into activated antimicrobial resistance of in situ hospital-wastewater biofilm
Risk ranking and antimicrobial resistance of Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli of bovine origin
Remote realities: In-depth conversations on antimicrobial stewardship in remote Indigenous communities using a One Health approach
Sewage surveillance for assessing clinical antibiotic resistance prevalence: Combining metagenomic and phenotypic data
abstract: Surveillance of antibiotic resistance in clinical isolates is a cornerstone for the management of bacterial infections but is limited in large parts of the world, often due to lack of resources. Sewage surveillance has been proposed as a promising, resource-efficient complement to the traditional surveillance approach based on samples from many individual patients. Both phenotypic data on resistance in sewage isolates and abundance of antibiotic resistance genes in sewage have been shown to correlate with resistance prevalence in clinical isolates. Here, we aimed to directly compare and combine an isolate-based and a gene-based sewage surveillance approach to evaluate what best can reflect clinical resistance rates. The two approaches, based on susceptibility testing of collectedisolates and metagenomic sequencing, respectively, were applied to municipal sewage samples collected in ten European countries. The data generated was related to available data on resistance to aminopenicillins, fluoroquinolones, third generation cephalosporins and aminoglycosides prevalence in clinicalisolates using beta regression models. None of the tested individual predictors were superior across all four investigated classes of antibiotics. For modelling of aminopenicillin resistance, a clearly higher Rvalue was obtained when isolate-based and gene-based data was combined as predictors, also after adjusting for the number of included variables. We conclude that there could be a value of including both isolate- and gene-based sewage data for predictions of resistance rates in clinical isolates, while emphasizing the value of linking predictors to specific species and classes of antibiotics.

title: Clonal diversity, virulence factors and antibiotic resistance genes of Enterococcus faecalis and Klebsiella pneumoniae from urban rats in Malaysia
abstract: Peridomestic rats serve as important carriers of zoonotic pathogens, including multidrug-resistant bacteria such asand. However, information on the clonal diversity, antibiotic resistance, and virulence of these pathogens in wild urban rats remains limited, particularly in tropical settings. This study investigatedandin urban rats from wet markets across four Malaysian states. A total of 277 rats (, = 177;, = 100) were trapped, and lung tissues were processed for bacterial isolation. Isolates were identified by 16S rDNA sequencing and examined for antibiotic susceptibility, resistance genes, and virulence factors using PCR. Clonal relationships were determined through multilocus sequence typing (MLST). Nineteenand sevenisolates were recovered. Allisolates carried multiple virulence factors (,,, and), and four tetracycline-resistant isolates possessed,, and. Five novelsequence types (ST730 - ST734) were identified. Allisolates carried the SHV gene; two also harbored FOX, and two possessedandvirulence factors. Two novelSTs (ST2641 and ST2642) were detected. Phylogenetic analyses revealed that both species displayed diverse sequence types scattered across global lineages. These findings suggest that urban rats may act as potential carriers of virulent and antibiotic-resistantand. These findings support the inclusion of urban rats in future One Health surveillance programs investigating antimicrobial resistance and virulent bacterial pathogens.

title: Virulence attenuation in ST11-K64 Klebsiella pneumoniae explains its divergent clinical manifestation from ST23-K1
Design, synthesis, and antibacterial activity study of pyrroloquinazoline diamine derivatives
Antimicrobial resistance patterns and polymicrobial co-detection characteristics of vaginal Group B Streptococcus in pregnant women: a retrospective study
Genetic determinants of hypervirulence with attenuated pathogenicity in a bla(NDM-1)-encoding Klebsiella pneumoniae causing neonatal sepsis
Copper-coated carbon nanotube surfaces for inhibiting biofilm formation by Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa
abstract: Biofilm-associated infections caused by clinically important pathogens such as() and() remain a major challenge in healthcare settings due to enhanced antimicrobial resistance and persistence. In recent years, copper-coated carbon nanotubes (Cu-CNTs) have gained considerable attention as promising antimicrobial nanomaterials for preventing biofilm formation on medical devices and hospital-associated surfaces. This review summarizes recent advances in the development and application of Cu-CNT-based antimicrobial coatings, with an emphasis on their antibacterial and antibiofilm activities against Gram-positive and Gram-negative pathogens. The synergistic combination of the high surface-area-to-volume ratio of CNTs and the potent antimicrobial properties of copper (Cu) ions enhances microbial inhibition. Previous studies suggest that Cu-CNTs interfere with initial bacterial adhesion, inhibit biofilm maturation, and disrupt established biofilms through mechanisms involving oxidative stress generation, membrane destabilization, and cellular damage. Furthermore, the review discusses the physicochemical characteristics, antimicrobial mechanisms, biomedical applications, and potential challenges associated with Cu-CNT coatings, including toxicity and biocompatibility concerns. Overall, Cu-CNT-based coatings represent a promising strategy for developing durable antimicrobial surfaces to control chronic biofilm-associated infections and reduce healthcare-associated contamination.

Differential modulation of gentamicin antibacterial activity by vitamin B12 and vitamin D3 against Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria: an in vitro-in silico study
Harnessing hydrogel technology for advanced periodontitis therapy: A multifunctional approach to oral health restoration
abstract: Periodontitis is a bacterially driven inflammatory disease that can lead to tooth mobility and tooth loss. Conventional non-surgical therapy, antibiotics, and surgery may be limited by residual subgingival biofilms, antimicrobial resistance, and variable clinical outcomes. This review synthesizes recent studies of hydrogel-based systems for local periodontal therapy, focusing on stimuli-responsive release mechanisms, cargo-loading approaches, and regenerative outcomes in relevant animal models. Across these studies, hydrogels function as localized delivery matrices that can prolong retention at periodontal defects, regulate therapeutic exposure, and support tissue repair. We further evaluate translational considerations, including degradation behavior, long-termstability, and immunocompatibility. These findings position hydrogels as adaptable platforms for more precise periodontitis management and identify priorities for preclinical optimization before clinical translation.

title: Microbiota-constrained bacterial density limits phage infection in the gut and allows persistence of susceptible cells
abstract: With the rise of antibiotic resistance, bacteriophage-based treatments against bacterial infections have regained momentum. However, phage therapy has so far shown only moderate success in complex environments like the mammalian gut, where phages are particularly promising tools for microbiome engineering and specific elimination of opportunistic pathogens. Here, we use different murine models of intestinal colonization to quantitatively assess the minimal population size of susceptiblecells that is required for phage replication in the gut (replication threshold). We found that the composition of the intestinal microbiota is a key factor shaping phage-bacteria interactions by restricting the carrying capacity of susceptible host cells. We further demonstrate that the replication threshold enables coexistence of susceptible and resistant bacteria in phage-treated mice, with implications for phage-based applications in complex environments like the gut.

Dihydromyricetin as an Antibiofilm and Antibacterial Agent Against Streptococcus agalactiae
abstract: (Group B) is a leading causative agent of sepsis, pneumonia and meningitis in neonates and is also a major pathogen responsible for bovine mastitis, posing a substantial threat to food safety and public health via the dairy production chain. The ability ofto form biofilms in the host enhances its resistance to conventional antibiotics and host immune defenses, thereby contributing to persistent and chronic infections. This study aimed to evaluate the antibacterial, antibiofilm, and combined antibacterial effects of dihydromyricetin (DMY) against thestrain GBS2 isolated from bovine mastitis. DMY exhibited significant antibacterial activity against GBS2, with a minimum inhibitory concentration and minimum bactericidal concentration of 0.5 mg/mL. Crystal violet staining and confocal laser scanning microscopy analyses demonstrated that DMY effectively inhibited and disrupted biofilm formation, resulting in looser and less dense biofilm structures compared to untreated controls. Furthermore, reverse transcription-quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) results revealed that DMY modulated the transcript levels of biofilm-associated genes (,,,, and). Additionally, DMY markedly potentiated the antibacterial effect of penicillin G, ciprofloxacin, oxacillin, and vancomycin. These findings suggest that DMY could serve as a natural antibiofilm agent for controllingcontamination in the dairy industry, thereby contributing to the prevention of foodborne infections and reducing reliance on conventional antibiotics.

title: Bioprocessing of Talaromyces purpurogenus for production of dihydromonascorubrin with a powerful antioxidant and antimicrobial activities integrated with the network-guided target prediction and molecular docking analyses
abstract: The antibiotic resistance of pathogenic microorganisms due to the irresponsible use in healthcare and agricultural practices is one of the global threats for the human, especially immune-compromised patients. Thus, searching for a novel compounds from fungi with unique affinity to combat the drug-resistant microorganisms was the objective. Talaromyces purpurogenus # PZ292970.1, an endophyte of palm tree Elaeis guineensis, has the highest productivity of azaphilone pigment (25.5 AU410/ml), with a strong activity against E. coli (MIC value 6.8 µg/ml), S. aureus and C. albicans (MIC value 12.5 µg/ml). The extracted pigment of T. purpurogenus has a strong antibiofilm activity for S. aureus (86.2%), C. albicans (85.8%) and E. coli (79.7%), compared to the control. The TLC purified-pigment of T. purpurogenus had a maximum absorbance at λnm, with a small one at λnm, revealing the identity of the major peak as orange azaphilone pigment. The purified pigment gave a distinct single peak by HPLC, ensures their structural homogeneity. From the FT-IR analyses, the absorption and stretching vibration of the target compound functional groups ensures their spectral identity as polyketide azaphilone. The 1HNMR and 13CNMR spectra revealed characteristic proton signals for the aromatic polyketide related to dihydromonascorubrin derivatives. From LC-MS/MS, the purified compound had 385.2 m/z that were matched to the molecular mass of dihydromonascorubrin, compared the authentic dihydromonascorubrin (382.4 m/z) as suggest from the fragmentation pattern by CFM-ID software. The yield of azaphilone pigment was increased by 2 folds upon bioprocessing by Plackett-Burman design, and by 2.4 folds by γ-irradiation at 1.0 kGy. The pigment showed a powerful antioxidant activity with free radical scavenging and reducing properties as reported by DPPH, ABT and FRAP assays. Integrating target prediction and molecular docking in silico analyses, dihydromonascorubrin exhibited multi-target mechanisms linked to efflux-associated resistance in E. coli and peptidoglycan remodeling in S. aureus.

title: National trends in antimicrobial consumption in Nepal, 2016-2023: an ecological analysis
abstract: To characterize class-specific national antimicrobial consumption patterns in Nepal from 2016 to 2023 and explore monotonic and linear temporal patterns, differences between the 2016-2019 and 2020-2023 periods, and the influence of selected high-consumption years. We conducted a retrospective ecological analysis of five antimicrobial classes using annual national consumption expressed as Defined Daily Doses per 1,000 inhabitants per day (DID). Descriptive statistics summarized consumption; Mann-Kendall tests and linear regression explored temporal patterns; an exploratory period comparison assessed 2016-2019 versus 2020-2023; and sensitivity analyses assessed the influence of selected years. Antibacterial agents had the highest mean consumption at 48.6 defined daily doses per 1,000 inhabitants per day (DID). Considerable year-to-year variability was observed across antimicrobial classes, with limited evidence of sustained temporal trends over the short observation period. Anti-tuberculosis drug consumption showed evidence of an upward monotonic pattern in the Mann-Kendall analysis. However, this finding was not supported by a statistically clear linear trend and was sensitive to exclusion of the 2023 value. Exploratory comparisons of the 2016-2019 and 2020-2023 period showed imprecisely estimated differences in antibacterial and antifungal consumption. National antimicrobial consumption in Nepal exhibited substantial class-specific and annual variation over 2016-2023. The short observation period constrains inference about sustained long-term trends. In particular, the apparent increase in anti-tuberculosis drug consumption warrants cautious interpretation given its sensitivity to 2023, rather than providing definitive evidence of a persistent increase.

title: Mitochondrial iron homeostasis is required for azole tolerance in Candida albicans
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is an escalating global concern with the human fungal pathogen, Candida albicans, increasingly exhibiting resistance to fluconazole (FLC). Together with the high mortality associated with bloodstream infections, this growing resistance contributed to the classification of C. albicans as a critical priority pathogen by the World Health Organisation (WHO). Notably, C. albicans can survive high concentrations of fluconazole (FLC) through a phenomenon termed tolerance, which is different from resistance as tolerant cells grow slowly. Tolerance is considered a precursor to resistance development. Previous work from our laboratory demonstrated that intracellular iron homeostasis, particularly the mobilisation of vacuolar iron stores, modulates the synergistic interaction between doxycycline, an iron chelator, and FLC. Building on this, we hypothesised that mitochondrial iron plays a central role in determining FLC susceptibility, supported by emerging links between mitochondrial function, iron metabolism, and azole response. Mitochondrial iron import is mediated by MRS4, after which iron is primarily incorporated into iron-sulfur clusters and haem. Here, we investigated the role of mitochondrial iron import via MRS4 in azole susceptibility phenotypes, including tolerance, synergy and cidality. We demonstrate that MRS4 is essential for FLC tolerance under iron-chelating conditions, despite minimal effects on minimal inhibitory concentration or drug synergy. Absence of MRS4 results in mitochondrial dysfunction and accumulation of toxic sterol intermediates during FLC treatment. Collectively, our findings reveal that mitochondrial iron homeostasis critically governs azole tolerance and highlights toxic sterol accumulation as a driver of fungicidal outcomes.

title: Integrative metabolomics and chemometric analysis reveal metabolites associated with antibacterial and antibiofilm activities of celery, Coriander, and parsley against multidrug-resistant uropathogenic Escherichia coli
abstract: The emergence of multidrug-resistant (MDR) uropathogenic Escherichia coli and the increasing prevalence of biofilm-associated infections have created an urgent need for new antimicrobial strategies. Celery (Apium graveolens L.), coriander (Coriandrum sativum L.), and parsley (Petroselinum crispum) are widely consumed herbs with reported medicinal properties; however, the relationship between their metabolite composition and antimicrobial potential remains insufficiently understood. This study investigated whether differences in the metabolite profiles of these Apiaceae herbs are associated with their antibacterial and antibiofilm activities against clinical MDR uropathogenic E. coli isolates. Methanolic extracts of celery, coriander, and parsley, together with their derived methylene chloride: water (50:50, v/v) fractions, were evaluated for antibacterial and antibiofilm activities against clinical MDR uropathogenic E. coli. Untargeted LC-QTOF-MS/MS metabolomics in positive and negative ionization modes was combined with multivariate chemometric analyses to characterize metabolite profiles, discriminate among the three herbs, and identify metabolites associated with the observed biological activities. A total of 167 metabolites were annotated, including flavonoids, coumarins, phenolic acids, fatty acids, chlorins, and amino acid derivatives. Chemometric analyses clearly differentiated the three Apiaceae species based on their metabolic composition. Coriander exhibited the strongest antibacterial activity, with a minimum inhibitory concentration of 3.75 µg/mL, while all tested extracts demonstrated significant inhibition of biofilm formation. Integration of metabolomic and bioactivity data highlighted hydroxylated fatty acids, quercetin derivatives, coumarins, chlorin-related metabolites, and eucommicin A as candidate metabolites associated with antibacterial and antibiofilm effects. This study provides the first integrated metabolomics-guided comparison of celery, coriander, and parsley against clinical MDR uropathogenic E. coli isolates. By linking metabolite signatures with antibacterial and antibiofilm activities, the findings offer new insight into the phytochemical basis of the biological effects of these edible herbs and identify promising candidates for future bioassay-guided and mechanistic studies aimed at combating antimicrobial resistance and biofilm-associated infections.

title: Antimicrobial resistance and chlorhexidine susceptibility in canine staphylococcal isolates from dogs with pyoderma and clinically healthy dogs
abstract: Staphylococci, particularly Staphylococcus pseudintermedius, are the major pathogens of canine pyoderma. Meanwhile, the emergence of antimicrobial resistance has become a global concern. Chlorhexidine digluconate is widely used antiseptic in veterinary medicine; however, recent studies on chlorhexidine susceptibility in veterinary staphylococci remain limited. This study evaluated the antimicrobial resistance, chlorhexidine digluconate susceptibility, and presence of antiseptic resistance-associated genes (qacA/B, qacG, and smr) in staphylococcal isolates from dogs with pyoderma and clinically healthy dogs in Korea. In total, 145 staphylococcal isolates were obtained, including S. pseudintermedius and S. schleiferi. Antimicrobial susceptibility was evaluated using the disk diffusion. Chlorhexidine digluconate susceptibility was determined using the microdilution, qacA/B and smr were detected using real-time PCR, and qacG was detected using conventional PCR. Of the 145 isolates, 93 (64.1%) were classified as multidrug-resistant (MDR). Chlorhexidine digluconate minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) ranged from 0.25 to 2 μg/mL, with no significant difference between MDR and non-MDR isolates. qacA/B, qacG, and smr were detected in 4, 13, and 10 isolates, respectively. Isolates carrying both qacA/B and smr showed relatively higher MICs; however, the number of positive isolates was small, and single-gene carriage was not clearly associated with increased MICs. Overall, the chlorhexidine digluconate MICs were substantially lower than the clinical concentrations, and antiseptic resistance-associated genes were detected at low frequencies. Despite the high frequency of MDR isolates, chlorhexidine digluconate remains a useful antiseptic option, although continuous monitoring of reduced susceptibility and antiseptic resistance-associated genes is warranted.

title: Community context redirects evolutionary trajectories under stress
abstract: Adaptation to abiotic stress is typically studied in single-species cultures, yet bacteria inhabit and evolve in multispecies communities where neighboring organisms reshape, for example, nutrient availability, redox state, and cellular physiology. We recently demonstrated that interspecies interactions can alter the fitness effects of antibiotic resistance mutations, and we suggest that this reflects a broader principle. Stress-response networks are extensively cross-regulated and draw upon a shared, finite pool of proteomic and energetic resources. Consequently, activation of one pathway constrains others, creating physiological trade-offs. Because microbial interactions routinely perturb the physiological inputs to these networks, they can systematically redirect evolutionary trajectories under abiotic stress. We discuss the evidence, limitations, and implications of this framework for predicting evolution and understanding microbiome stability.

title: Microbial resistance from genotype to metabolic phenotype
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses an escalating global threat, yet surveillance and mechanistic understanding remain anchored in individual resistance genes, an approach that is inadequate for capturing the ecological, genomic, and metabolic complexity through which resistance emerges and spreads. In this opinion article, we argue that genome-scale metabolic models (GEMs) offer a principled framework for advancing AMR research beyond this gene-centric paradigm. Strain-resolved GEMs embed resistance determinants within metabolic networks, with the potential to generate quantitative, context-dependent phenotypic predictions, including minimum inhibitory concentrations and environment-conditional resistance, that sequence-based tools do not provide. Expanded GEM frameworks incorporating mobile genetic elements, horizontal gene transfer, and community-level interactions support ecology-aware resistance profiling. At the therapeutic level, whole-network modelling can identify metabolic vulnerabilities, synthetic lethal interactions, and microbiome-targeted strategies. Integrating GEMs with multiomics and data-driven approaches represents a critical step toward a mechanism-aware AMR platform connecting surveillance, diagnosis, and drug discovery.

title: Supersulfides in bacterial antibiotic resistance: chemical inactivation, redox signaling, and translational opportunities
abstract: The global spread of antimicrobial-resistant bacteria has emerged as one of the most pressing public health challenges worldwide. Because the development of novel antibiotics remains slow and increasingly difficult, innovative therapeutic strategies are urgently needed. Supersulfides, including persulfides and polysulfides, are ubiquitous sulfur species found in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes. Owing to their exceptional nucleophilicity and antioxidant capacity, they play central roles in cellular redox signaling and stress adaptation. Recent studies have further revealed that bacterial supersulfides contribute to antibiotic resistance through multiple mechanisms, including the direct chemical inactivation of β-lactam antibiotics, activation of multidrug efflux pumps, and detoxification of reactive oxygen species generated during antibiotic treatment. These findings identify bacterial supersulfide biosynthetic pathways as promising targets for the development of next-generation antimicrobial therapies. In this Review, we summarize current knowledge of supersulfide biosynthesis, with particular emphasis on recently identified pathways unique to bacteria. We also discuss the diverse mechanisms by which bacterial supersulfides promote antibiotic resistance and highlight recent advances in pharmacological strategies targeting supersulfide biosynthesis. Finally, we discuss the translational potential of targeting bacterial supersulfide metabolism and the key challenges that must be overcome for clinical application.

title: Does transfusion of blood products increase the risk of multidrug-resistant infections in critically ill patients?
abstract: To investigate the association between transfusion of blood products during intensive care unit (ICU) stay and the incidence of ICU-acquired colonisation and infection with multidrug-resistant (MDR) bacteria (ICU-MDR-col, ICU-MDR-inf, respectively). Secondary analysis of two prospective multicentre cohort studies conducted in eight ICUs in France. Adult patients admitted to participating ICUs were enrolled consecutively from May 2019 to June 2021. All patients underwent systematic screening for colonisation with MDR bacteria at admission and weekly thereafter. Exposure to transfusion of blood products during ICU stay, including packed red blood cells (PRBCs), fresh frozen plasma (FFP) and platelet concentrates (PCs), was recorded. The primary outcome was the incidence of ICU-MDR-col and/or ICU-MDR-inf (ICU-MDR-col/inf) until ICU discharge, censored at day 28. Secondary outcomes included the incidence of ICU-MDR-col and ICU-MDR-inf, considered separately. Associations were assessed using mixed-effects Poisson regression models adjusted for prespecified confounders. Subgroup analyses were performed according to immunosuppression status at ICU admission. Among 1103 patients, 358 (32.5%) received transfusion of any blood product. Overall, 292 (26.5%) patients experienced at least one ICU-MDR-col/inf event. Transfusion was associated with an increased incidence of ICU-MDR-col/inf (adjusted incidence rate ratio [aIRR] 1.31, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.06-1.62; p = 0.013), mainly driven by ICU-MDR-inf (aIRR 1.62, 95% CI 1.16-2.24; p = 0.004), but not ICU-MDR-col considered individually. This association was restricted to PRBC transfusion. No significant heterogeneity was observed according to immunosuppression status. Transfusion of PBRCs was associated with an increased incidence of ICU-acquired MDR infections, with no significant heterogeneity observed according to immunosuppression status. These findings support a restrictive approach to transfusion and warrant further investigation into its immunological and ecological consequences in critically ill patients.

title: Emergence of Candida (Candidozyma) auris in Warming Climates
abstract: ()is a pathogenic fungus first identified in a patient in 2009. Prior to this clinical finding,was unknown, with its closest relative being the marine-dwellingInfections are increasing annually, predominately impacting hospital patients due to durable biofilms on medical devices and antimicrobial resistance. Perplexingly, the fungus arose nearly simultaneously across the globe in independent disease emergences from six genetically distinct clades. Theclades mostly diverged from one another 5,000-10,000 years ago, during a period when global temperatures and sea levels rose and coastal wetlands flourished. Within the past 200-300 years, a new wave of rapid divergence occurred within each clade. This corresponds to industrialization, urbanization, global warming, and the widespread wetland destruction. Environmental stressors, including heat, are hypothesized to have driven mutations and stress resistance. These may not only helpwithstand a changing climate but also help it thrive within mammalian hosts.

title: How do we monitor doxy-PEP impact and when should we consider revisiting guidelines?
abstract: The 2026 WHO guidelines recommending doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis (doxy-PEP) represent the first global antibiotic prophylaxis recommendation for bacterial sexually transmitted infections (STIs), with provisions for antimicrobial resistance (AMR) monitoring.Doxy-PEP should be governed as an adaptive intervention subject to periodic, transparent review, but establishing decision rules faces challenges.Doxy-PEP is expected to select for resistance, including in Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Staphylococcus aureus, and the gut and skin microbiomes; the scope of clinical consequences is incompletely understood.As STI prevalence falls, the benefit per dose declines while the AMR externality per dose is expected to grow, shifting the cost-benefit balance in ways that vary across populations and settings.Attributing changes in disease prevalence or resistance patterns to doxy-PEP is methodologically difficult, given incompletely understood and complex drivers of pre-existing trends, surveillance limitations, and heterogeneous uptake, raising questions about study designs, data sources, eligibility criteria, and governance mechanisms.A full accounting of benefits and harms is broader than reduced bacterial STI incidence and AMR. Benefits include consideration of patient-centered outcomes such as reduced anxiety regarding STI acquisition, avoidance of repeated treatment visits, and fewer STI-related complications. Harms include drug side effects, such as gastrointestinal adverse effects and concerns about use in pregnancy.

title: Analysis of the impact of naturally-acquired immunity on Shigella vaccine performance to inform clinical trials: A simulation-based modeling study
abstract: Effective vaccines against Shigella, the leading bacterial cause of diarrheal disease globally, could prevent morbidity and mortality from shigellosis as well as limit antibiotic resistance. Several Shigella vaccine candidates are in late stages of development, and the design of large Phase 3 trials in target populations is underway. In high incidence settings, children are expected to rapidly accrue natural immunity such that after repeated pathogen exposure, unvaccinated infants may have similar levels of immunity as vaccinated infants. For this reason, in these settings estimates of vaccine efficacy (VE) may underestimate expected efficacy in a fully naïve population. To set expectations and support optimal planning of future Shigella vaccine trials, we aimed to quantify the potential impact of this phenomenon on VE estimates under different surveillance strategies and assumptions about Shigella immunity. We simulated Shigella vaccine trials in low-, medium-, and high-burden settings under different assumptions about vaccine- and infection-conferred immunity. We estimated VE against severe, Shigella-attributable disease and any Shigella-attributable diarrhea under six trial designs: active surveillance for Shigella infection or symptom-based reporting paired with single-outcome, stratified recurrent outcome, or crude recurrent-outcome Cox proportional hazards models. In each scenario, we evaluated bias, 95% confidence interval (CI) coverage, and the false negative rate. Only the trial design using active surveillance for infection and single outcome models was consistently unbiased across all examined scenarios. The other five designs underestimated VE by up to an absolute 20%, with a single outcome model paired with symptom-based reporting performing least poorly. Bias generally was worse at higher-burden sites. For realistically sized trials, the 95% CI coverage and false negative rate were also worse at higher-burden sites. The results were sensitive to input parameters which depended on assumptions about Shigella natural history based on limited published data. The observed VE in Shigella vaccine trials is likely to underestimate true VE, though the magnitude of underestimation described here is conditional on the simulation's inputs and assumptions. Careful trial design is needed to minimize this underestimation.

title: Genomic Exploration of CRISPR-Cas Systems in Raoultella species: Diversity and Architecture
abstract: Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats and CRISPR-associated protein (CRISPR-Cas) systems are adaptive immune mechanisms that protect bacteria against invading mobile genetic elements. They can influence horizontal gene transfer, phage resistance, and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) dynamics. Although these systems have been investigated in several Klebsiella species, information on historically defined Raoultella species remains limited. In this study, 103 complete genomes representing Raoultella species, currently placed within the broader Klebsiella lineage, were analyzed to characterize the distribution, architecture, and diversity of CRISPR-Cas systems. CRISPR-Cas loci were identified using CRISPRCasFinder and CRISPRone, followed by subtype classification, direct repeat and leader sequence analyses, spacer matching, Cas1-based phylogenetic analysis, and AMR determinant screening. Complete CRISPR-Cas systems were detected in 23 genomes, predominantly in R. ornithinolytica strains. All complete systems were chromosomally located, whereas plasmid-associated orphan CRISPR arrays were observed in selected R. ornithinolytica strains. Two major architectures were identified, with Type I-E being dominant and Type I-F restricted to fewer strains. Direct repeat analysis revealed six consensus sequences, while leader regions displayed conserved AT-rich motifs and strain-specific divergence. Spacer analyses suggested historical interactions with phages and plasmids, particularly mobile genetic elements associated with Klebsiella and other Enterobacteriaceae. Cas1 phylogeny showed subtype-dependent clustering, indicating that CRISPR-Cas evolution does not strictly follow core genome phylogeny. The coexistence of predicted CRISPR-Cas loci and AMR determinants indicates that the presence of these loci does not necessarily preclude the carriage of resistance determinants. Overall, this study expands current knowledge of CRISPR-Cas diversity among the analyzed Raoultella genomes and provides a genomic framework for future functional studies.

title: Expanding threat of carbapenemase-producing Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae in Peru: genomic and phenotypic evidence of high-risk clones dissemination
abstract: Carbapenemase-producingrepresent a growing global threat due to their extensive antimicrobial resistance and rapid dissemination. This study characterized the phenotypic and genomic features ofandisolates collected between 2020 and 2022 from four healthcare institutions in Lima, Peru. A total of 320 non-redundant isolates (61and 259) were analyzed through antimicrobial susceptibility testing, polymerase chain reaction, and whole-genome sequencing. The most frequent carbapenemase gene was(69%), followed by(16.9%) and(4.6%). Elevenisolates co-produced NDM and KPC, and oneisolate co-harbored NDM and OXA-48-like. All isolates were multidrug-resistant, and 5% were resistant to all agents included in the routine panel; however, aztreonam/avibactam and cefiderocol retained completeactivity among tested isolates. Novel β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations such as aztreonam/avibactam and cefiderocol showed complete activity against all classes of carbapenemases. Genomic analysis revealed predominantsequence types ST167 and ST410 andlineages ST147, ST15, ST45, and ST273. Theallele was detected for the first time in Peru, mostly in, and was carried on multireplicon IncF-type plasmids. In, ST147 was identified as a dominant clone associated with, indicating sustained local dissemination of high-risk clonal groups. The coexistence of multiple carbapenemases and plasmid backbones highlights the ongoing evolution of resistance mechanisms. This work provides the first integrative genomic overview of carbapenemase-producingandin Peru and underscores the need for continuous genomic surveillance and antimicrobial stewardship to mitigate their clinical and epidemiological impact.

title: Purification and mechanistic characterisation of bacillomycin D homologues from Bacillus velezensis PD9 with antibiofilm activity against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance continues to undermine treatment of multidrug-resistant infections, necessitating new antimicrobial agents with distinct mechanisms of action. Bacillus velezensis PD9 (BvPD9), isolated from Heterotrigona itama propolis, produces antibacterial lipopeptides; however, the active bacillomycin D homologues and their mechanisms remain insufficiently characterised. Here, an optimised extraction and chromatographic purification workflow was developed, enabling selective enrichment of two bioactive fractions putatively assigned by LC-TOF-MS/MS as C14-enriched bacillomycin D and a C14/C15-bacillomycin D homologue mixture. The C14-enriched bacillomycin D fraction exhibited selective activity against Staphylococcus spp. and vancomycin-sensitive Enterococcus faecium (VSEF), with minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of 16-32 µg/mL, whereas the C14/C15 homologue mixture demonstrated broader antibacterial activity against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and selected ESKAPE pathogens (Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Enterobacter spp.) (MICs 16-512 µg/mL), with the lowest MIC (16 µg/mL) observed against VSEF. Both compounds retained activity following heat exposure (40-80 °C), wide pH variation (4-12), and proteolytic enzymes. The C14/C15 homologue mixture was prioritised for further evaluation because of its broader antibacterial spectrum and displayed concentration-dependent inhibition of biofilm formation, membrane permeabilisation, and ultrastructural alterations, together with changes in bacterial DNA-content distribution without detectable direct DNA binding. Preliminary safety evaluation demonstrated concentration-dependent haemolysis and cytotoxicity at higher concentrations, while zebrafish embryos showed concentration-dependent mortality with an LCof 109.54 µg/mL at 120 hpf. Serial passaging resulted in a four-fold MIC increase only during the final passages, whereas chloramphenicol showed no detectable MIC change under the same conditions. Overall, the findings demonstrate antibacterial and membrane-associated activities of PD9-derived bacillomycin D-enriched fractions and provide a basis for further investigation of individually purified homologues.

title: Meeting gene expression demand during evolution of antibiotic resistance
abstract: Regulated gene expression in bacteria accommodates demands imposed by different environments. In addition to ensuring the production of required metabolic and structural components, gene regulation protects bacteria against the adverse effects of misexpression. Upon encountering a novel environment, such as sustained exposure to antibiotics, transcriptional recalibration ensues to improve fitness. For antibiotics, this involves enhancing the expression of an existing repertoire of resistance mechanisms and is often mediated by mutations in regulators of gene expression. Here, we review how diverse gene regulatory mutations confer antibiotic resistance to bacterial pathogens. We view these strategies through the lens of the Gene Expression Demand Theory, originally proposed for inducible operons involved in sugar metabolism, and describe the molecular basis and evolutionary consequences for a few well-studied examples. Broad underlying preferences of when and which kind of regulatory mutations bacteria employ emerge from these examples. A key pattern appears to be a preference for derepression rather than activating mutations, and we highlight potential underlying genetic and evolutionary explanations. Finally, even as our knowledge of molecular mechanisms of antibiotic adaptation continues to expand, we propose that adaptation by regulatory mutations provides a framework for assessing the risk of resistance evolution in the case of novel antibiotics and alternative targets for diagnostic and therapeutic interventions.

title: Physicochemical characterization of a bioactive Minthostachys verticillata nanoemulsion with enhanced antibacterial efficacy against veterinary pathogens
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance among livestock pathogens represents a growing challenge for veterinary medicine, underscoring the need for effective plant-based alternatives. This study describes the development and physicochemical characterization of an oil-in-water nanoemulsion incorporatingessential oil (EO) and evaluates its biocompatibility and antibacterial efficacy. The EO, obtained by steam distillation (yield 4.8% v/w), was chemically characterized by GC-MS, revealing a pulegone-menthone chemotype. A series of nanoemulsion formulations were prepared by modulating surfactant composition and processing parameters, leading to the selection of an optimized formulation (NE2-S). This nanoemulsion exhibited a mean droplet size of 103.2 nm, low polydispersity (PDI = 0.279), and moderate electrostatic stabilization, complemented by steric stabilization provided by non-ionic surfactants (ζ-potential = -22.5 mV). Biocompatibility assessment using an MTT assay in murine fibroblasts demonstrated low cytotoxicity at concentrations up to 2500 μg/mL. Antibacterial evaluation against enterotoxigenic(ETEC) andrevealed enhanced efficacy of NE2-S compared with EO, with two-fold reductions in both minimum inhibitory and bactericidal concentrations. Biofilm inhibition and eradication assays were additionally performed against the same field isolates. NE2-S showed a clear advantage over EO in inhibiting and eradicating ETEC F4+ biofilm, whereas its effect againstbiofilm was more limited, with EO proving superior at eradicating pre-formedbiofilm. Overall, these findings establish a physicochemical framework linking nanoscale colloidal architecture to improved antibacterial performance, supporting the potential of this nanoemulsion platform as a promising antimicrobial strategy for the control of bacterial infections of veterinary relevance in livestock production.

title: Travel-associated Staphylococcus aureus infections: a global perspective from the GeoSentinel Surveillance Network
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major global health threat, and Staphylococcus aureus is among the leading contributors to the global AMR-attributable disease burden. Data on the clinical presentation and antimicrobial susceptibility patterns of Staphylococcus aureus infections in returning travellers remain scarce. We described the clinical presentation, travel characteristics, and antimicrobial susceptibility of travellers and migrants diagnosed with Staphylococcus aureus infection through the GeoSentinel network between January 2014 and December 2022. Because no consensus definition exists for travel-associated infections, we included all cases recorded in the GeoSentinel database as travel-associated. We evaluated patients during travel or after return. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) was performed according to routine laboratory practice at participating sites. We retrieved 740 travellers and migrants with Staphylococcus aureus infection diagnosed at 50 GeoSentinel sites. Four hundred thirty-eight (59.2%) were male, and the median age was 32 years (IQR 23-48). The most frequently visited regions were Southeast Asia, sub-Saharan Africa, and South-Central Asia. Most patients presented after travel (576/740; 77.8%). Skin and soft tissue infections were the predominant diagnosis (670/740; 90.5%), and most patients were managed as outpatients (579/740; 78.2%).
