Overall, 406/740 (54.9%) isolates showed resistance or reduced susceptibility to at least one antimicrobial class, including methicillin (224/656; 34.1%), lincosamides (144/627; 23.0%), and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (129/597; 21.6%). Demographic characteristics and hospitalization frequency were similar between patients with MSSA and MRSA infections. Most Staphylococcus aureus infections in international travellers presented as skin and soft tissue infections and were managed in outpatient settings. Resistance or reduced susceptibility to at least one antimicrobial class was common, with one-third of isolates identified as methicillin-resistant. These findings support the importance of AST to guide management of skin and soft tissue infections in internationally mobile populations and reinforce the need for standardized definitions of travel-associated bacterial infections and continued global surveillance.

title: Solving the Staphylococcus aureus puzzle: lessons to guide future MRSA vaccine development
abstract: SUMMARYThe broad-spectrum use of antibiotics allows for the development of resistance in symptomatically and asymptomatically carried pathogenic bacteria. Antibiotic-resistant bacteria, with this review focusing on, cause significant morbidity and mortality and put considerable strain on the global healthcare system. In a vaccinated individual, bacteria are less likely to develop resistance mechanisms compared to an individual treated with antibiotics, highlighting a potential method for conserving antibiotic use. However, despite over a century of research, avaccine candidate is yet to progress past phase III clinical trials, and to develop a successfulvaccine, the shortcomings of previous attempts require critical analysis. After consideration of the five most successfulvaccine programs, it is identified in this review that future attempts should (i) be polyvalent to circumvent immune evasion, (ii) include carefully chosen antigens to avoid maladaptive memory, (iii) include T cell targeting to provide a comprehensive immune response, (iv) utilize multiple measures of preclinical efficacy in pre-exposed models, and (v) implement considered clinical study design, including appropriate vaccine formulation for the target population. By combining these attributes, such as in the form of epitope-based or nanoparticle vaccines, there is a promising future for the development ofvaccines that circumvent the issues that caused the downfall of previous vaccine programs, thereby protecting the global population from development toward a future where bacteria are resistant to all antibiotic treatments.

title: Wildlife-associated ecosystems in Algeria harbor internationally distributed ESBL-producing clones and plasmids, including a CTX-M-15 Klebsiella pneumoniae ST17 lineage associated with a conserved IncFIB(K) resistance plasmid
abstract: Expanded-spectrum cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales (ESC-R-E) have disseminated beyond clinical settings, but their occurrence and genomic epidemiology in wildlife remain poorly characterized, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. ESC-R may result from the production of extended-spectrum β-lactamases (ESBLs) or AmpC-type cephalosporinases. We investigated the prevalence, resistance mechanisms, and population structure of ESC-R-E in free-ranging wildlife, captive wild animals, and zoo workers in Algeria. Between October 2021 and June 2023, 1,899 fecal samples were collected across six Algerian provinces. ESC-R-E isolates were recovered by selective culture and characterized by antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and whole-genome sequencing. Overall, 73 ESC-R-E isolates (3.9%) were identified, including seven OXA-48-like carbapenemase co-producers (0.4%). Carriage was significantly higher in captive animals (13.5%) than in free-ranging wildlife (1.6%) or zoo workers (7.7%). Among the 66 ESBL-producing isolates analyzed, CTX-M enzymes predominated (= 61), particularly CTX-M-15 (= 53).was the predominant species (= 33), with ST17 accounting for 27/33 isolates. Closely related CTX-M-15-producing ST17 isolates were recovered from captive animals, free-ranging wildlife, and a zoo worker and carried an IncFIB(K) plasmid harboringwithin a multidrug resistance region closely related to globally disseminated plasmids. Globally disseminated high-riskclones were also detected, namely ST167, ST361, ST410, and a persistent ST38 lineage in Algerian wildlife since 2016. These findings demonstrate the circulation of high-risk Enterobacterales lineages and mobile resistance plasmids in Algerian wildlife-associated ecosystems and highlight the need for integrated One Health surveillance of antimicrobial resistance at the human-animal-environment interface. Wildlife is increasingly recognized as a potential reservoir and sentinel for antimicrobial resistance, yet genomic data from low- and middle-income countries remain scarce. This study provides one of the largest genomic investigations of expanded-spectrum cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales in wildlife from North Africa. We demonstrate that internationally disseminated high-riskandlineages, together with globally distributed CTX-M-15-carrying plasmids, are circulating among captive animals, free-ranging wildlife, and humans in zoological environments. The recovery of closely relatedST17 isolates from different host species highlights the potential for antimicrobial resistance dissemination across the human-animal-environment interface. These findings extend the known ecological range of clinically important resistant Enterobacterales beyond healthcare settings and identify wildlife-associated ecosystems as part of the broader antimicrobial resistance network. Our study underscores the value of integrating wildlife into One Health surveillance programs to better understand and mitigate the environmental spread of antimicrobial resistance.

title: Antidepressant desvenlafaxine identified in wastewater promotes transformation and antibiotic resistance risk in Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1 via metabolic adaptations
abstract: Wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) are known reservoirs of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs). Non-antibiotic compounds, such as antidepressants, may further promote ARG acquisition through horizontal gene transfer (HGT). Desvenlafaxine, a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) listed on the EU Surface Water Watch List, is among the most frequently detected antidepressants in WWTP effluents, yet its role in HGT has not been examined. Here, we detected desvenlafaxine at the highest concentrations among four antidepressants monitored across three municipal WWTPs in western New York. UsingADP1 as a model recipient in natural transformation assays (= 6), we found that desvenlafaxine significantly increased transformation frequency at 10 mg/L (1.74 ± 0.33-fold) and 50 mg/L (1.49 ± 0.19-fold;< 0.05). Effects occurred without induction of reactive oxygen species or loss of membrane integrity, consistent with its very low toxicity (IC~1,300 mg/L). Instead, desvenlafaxine induced dose-dependent increases in membrane fluidity and shifts to less negative zeta potentials, suggesting that electrostatic interactions between its cationic amine group and the negatively charged membrane reduce surface repulsion and facilitate plasmid proximity during uptake. Non-targeted proteomics revealed a biphasic response: at 10 mg/L, competence-associated proteins (PilB, ComM) were upregulated, and STRING analysis identified networks linked to membrane transport, transcriptional regulation, and envelope remodeling, while no connected network was recovered at 50 mg/L. Electron microscopy confirmed higher pilus frequency at both doses. Together, these findings reveal a non-oxidative, envelope-mediated route by which a widely detected antidepressant increases bacterial competence.IMPORTANCEThe spread of antibiotic resistance poses a serious and escalating threat to human health worldwide. While antibiotic use is widely recognized as a key driver, non-antibiotic pharmaceuticals released into the environment through wastewater have received far less attention. Antidepressants are among the most frequently detected drugs in treated wastewater effluents, yet their potential to promote antibiotic resistance transfer in bacteria remains poorly understood. This study demonstrates that desvenlafaxine, one of the most abundant antidepressants found in municipal wastewater, can increase the uptake of antibiotic resistance genes in an environmental bacterium at concentrations above those currently measured in effluent, and identifies the bacterial cell-surface changes that enable this without cytotoxicity.

title: Exploring antimicrobial resistance in wild and domestic animal populations: combining publicly available data with BV-BRC resources to introduce bioinformatics in an undergraduate classroom
abstract: Bioinformatics blends the fields of biology, statistics, computer science, and information technology for the processing and analysis of genomic data. Despite the growing demand for trained bioinformaticians and a positive job market outlook, most undergraduate institutions struggle to integrate bioinformatics into their life science curricula. Educators face numerous barriers to incorporating bioinformatics into their classes, including technical issues and expertise. To address this need, we are developing web-accessible, course-based materials for general microbiology, infectious disease, genomics, and other similar undergraduate and graduate classes that use bioinformatic workflows within the Bacterial and Viral Bioinformatics Resource Center (BV-BRC), one of three National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID)-funded Bioinformatics Resource Centers. Here, we present one such activity: a three-part exercise focused on antimicrobial resistance and metagenomics that uses six publicly available metagenomic samples collected from wild and domestic animal populations to explore the distinctions between their gut microbiomes and their respective antibiotic resistance genes. To analyze community composition and identify antibiotic resistance genes, students use two end-to-end services offered by the BV-BRC: Taxonomic Classification and Metagenomic Read Mapping. This assignment was developed to introduce students to core competencies in the field of bioinformatics and to highlight the BV-BRC as an educational resource for integrating bioinformatics without requiring students and instructors to possess the technical proficiencies and computing resources traditionally needed. We successfully implemented this exercise in an upper-level undergraduate microbiology course, demonstrating the feasibility of using the BV-BRC for bioinformatics education in the classroom.

title: Differential impacts of early, extended-spectrum, and last-resort β-lactams on manure-derived microbiomes and resistomes in an in vitro model
abstract: Understanding the environmental dissemination of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is crucial for mitigating its spread and reducing the clinical burden of resistant infections. In a previous study, we demonstrated that copiotrophic enrichment in a medium that stimulates the growth of gut-associated bacteria can reveal clinically associated bacterial populations and antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) that are not detected through direct environmental sampling. In the present study, we applied this enrichment approach to poultry manure to examine how β-lactamase-resistant antibiotics (cefotaxime and meropenem) shape the composition and resistance profiles of copiotrophic, gut-like microbial community relative to an earlier β-lactam (ampicillin) and to antibiotic-free controls. Our results show that extended-spectrum and last-resort β-lactams induced more pronounced shifts in microbial diversity, resistome, and mobilome profiles compared to ampicillin. When focusing on specific taxa, such as clinically relevant enteric bacteria and both susceptible and β-lactam-resistant coliforms, differential responses were observed correlating to the antimicrobial range of action. Moreover, cefotaxime and meropenem exerted different effects on the relative abundance of enteric bacteria and plasmids harboring multiple ARGs. Together, these findings underline how the diversity of pathogen and AMR indicators in gut microbiomes may be shaped by different selective pressures imposed by β-lactamase-resistant antibiotics.IMPORTANCEThis study explores how different generations of β-lactam antibiotics shape microbial communities and antibiotic resistance in a gut-likesystem. Using a metabolically driven synthetic community derived from manure, we found that advanced β-lactams such as cefotaxime and meropenem led to stronger and more specific shifts in both community composition and resistance gene profiles compared to ampicillin. These results emphasize that the ecological impact of antibiotics depends not only on whether bacteria are inhibited but also on the spectrum of activity of each compound. In addition, the system we used provides a simple and controllable way to study interactions among antibiotics, microbial communities, and the resistome. Overall, this work offers a clearer ecological view of how clinically important antibiotics may influence microbiomes and the spread of antibiotic resistance genes.

title: Genomic insights into non-tuberculous mycobacteria isolated from patients in a Chinese hospital
abstract: Non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) are increasingly recognized as important opportunistic pathogens, yet the genomic basis of their antimicrobial resistance and virulence in clinical settings remains incompletely understood. We performed whole-genome sequencing on 28 clinical isolates of NTM collected from Chinese patients (primarily bronchoalveolar lavage fluid) between 2022 and 2025, combined with broth microdilution susceptibility testing and comprehensive bioinformatics analysis. The collection comprised diverse species, including,,,,,,, and. Phenotypic testing revealed extensive multidrug resistance: 100% of isolates were resistant to rifampicin, erythromycin, imipenem, and doxycycline; 82.1% were resistant to ciprofloxacin; 89.3% were resistant to linezolid; and only amikacin retained substantial activity (50% susceptible). Resistome profiling using the Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database/Resistance Gene Identifier identified heterogeneous distributions of efflux pumps (tap), ribosomal methylases [Erm(39)], β-lactamases (blaF), and other determinants, consistent with both intrinsic and accessory-genome-mediated resistance. Virulence factor annotation against the Virulence Factor Database revealed 531 unique factors, with hierarchical clustering separating isolates into two major clades: (i) rapid-growing species (and) enriched in secretion systems (ESX/T7SS), polyketide synthases, and lipid biosynthesis genes, and (ii) slow-growingcomplex species showing lower overall virulence gene abundance. Pangenome analysis indicated a relatively closed pangenome structure, with 1,026 core genes and substantial shell/cloud compartments contributing to strain-specific adaptations. These findings provide genomic insights into the multidrug-resistant and virulence-heterogeneous nature of contemporary Chinese clinical isolates of NTM.IMPORTANCEIn this study, we sequenced 28 clinical non-tuberculous mycobacterial strains, performed comprehensive drug susceptibility testing, and analyzed virulence factors to elucidate genomic determinants of resistance and pathogenicity, as well as evolutionary characteristics. These findings aim to bridge existing knowledge gaps, informing improved diagnostic and therapeutic strategies for non-tuberculous mycobacterial infections.

title: Antimicrobial Resistance Trends in COVID-19 Patients with Hospital Infection in Intensive Care: A Retrospective Study in Central Italy, 2020-2022
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) was exacerbated by COVID-19 pandemic. This study describes prevalence and trends of AMR in patients with diagnosed severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection admitted during 2020-2022 to the intensive care unit (ICU) in Molise region, central Italy. A retrospective study was conducted, including patients aged ≥ 18 years with at least one positive bacterial or fungal culture during ICU stay. Data were related to patient demographics, ICU outcomes, healthcare-associated infections, and antimicrobial susceptibility profiles. During the 2020-2022 period, 103 ICU admissions met the inclusion criteria, yielding 268 isolations, of which 157 underwent antimicrobial susceptibility testing. Apart from high proportion of, Gram-negative bacteria predominated, with,,, andamong the most frequent. Resistance to beta-lactams and carbapenems was consistently high, while it ranged from 53.8% to 66.7% to fluoroquinolones and remained above 50% to aminoglycosides. Tetracycline resistance showed significant year-to-year variation, increasing in 2022 compared with both 2020 and 2021. AMR rates in COVID-19 patients in ICU were persistently high throughout the pandemic, with critical resistance levels in Gram-negatives, underlining the need to reinforce infection prevention and control measures and antimicrobial stewardship programs and align prescribing practices with World Health Organization AWaRe recommendations, even during public health emergencies.

title: Hybrid membrane vesicle-enabled sonodynamic therapy using ciprofloxacin for treating biofilm-associated infections
abstract: Biofilm-associated infections on indwelling medical devices pose significant clinical challenges due to antibiotic resistance and poor drug penetration. Sonodynamic therapy (SDT) is a promising strategy utilizing ultrasound to activate sonosensitizers for generating reactive oxygen species (ROS). However, the lack of safe and effective sonosensitizers and bacterial-targeting delivery systems limits its application in treating biofilm infection. To address these limitations, we developed antibiotic ciprofloxacin-loaded hybrid membrane vesicles (CIP@HMVs), where ciprofloxacin acts as a safe sonosensitizer and HMVs serve as a detoxified bacterial-targeted delivery system. HMVs were engineered by fusing-derived outer membrane vesicles (PAEVs) with macrophage membrane vesicles (MMVs), creating a dual-functional nanoplatform with homotypic bacteria-targeting and detoxification capabilities. CIP@HMVs exploited ciprofloxacin's sonosensitizer properties to generate singlet oxygen (O) under ultrasound, while HMVs enhanced bacterial uptake in. This enabled synergistic bactericidal effects against planktonic bacteriamembrane disruption and intracellular ROS burst, achieving a 5.7-log bacterial reduction in catheter biofilms. Crucially, HMVs neutralized PAEVs' LPS toxicityand demonstrated negligible systemic toxicity. In a murine catheter-infection model, CIP@HMVs under ultrasound achieved 99.8% bacterial eradication and reduced inflammation. This bacterial-targeting sonodynamic platform provides a transformative strategy for treating device-associated biofilm infections with high efficacy and biosafety.

title: In silico analysis of SCO, an almost undescribed family of β-lactamases
abstract: β-lactamases rank amongst the most common mechanisms of antibiotic resistance, accounting for thousands of different variants. Current genomic tools have resulted in an exponential growth of new variants, most of which, as is the case for SCO, remain undescribed or non-characterised. This study aimed to detect new variants of SCO in GenBank records. The amino acid sequence of SCO-1 was compared with what is present in GenBank. Only amino acid sequences with >85% identity were considered. No synthetic or partial sequences were included in the analyses. Eleven different SCO variants were detected, 9 of which had previously not been designated as specific variants. Several of the modifications suggested the possible expansion of substrates towards 3rd and 4th generation cephalosporins or the resistance to inhibitors, while others might impair SCO functionality. SCO β-lactamases were detected in 6 bacterial families accounting for 14 genera. The presence of undescribed SCO variants in GenBank is reported, and the need to establish the exact substrate profile of new variants is highlighted.

title: NMR-Based Structural Elucidation of a New Dihydroisocoumarin and Related Polyketides From a Mangrove-Derived Fusarium sp
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) remains one of the greatest global public health challenges of the 21st century, compromising the effectiveness of current therapies and highlighting the urgent need for new antibacterial agents. Natural products from bacteria and filamentous fungi continue to represent an invaluable source of structurally diverse bioactive metabolites. In this study, a library of 56 extracts obtained from mangrove-associated ascomycetes was screened against a panel of multidrug-resistant bacterial pathogens. Bioactivity data were integrated with LC-MS/MS-based molecular networking to prioritize extracts for chemical investigation. This approach identified Fusarium sp. IQ-1921 as one of the most promising candidates, leading to the isolation of a new dihydroisocoumarin (1) and four known analogues (2-5). The structures of all isolated metabolites were elucidated by 1D and 2D NMR spectroscopy and high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS). All compounds were evaluated against multidrug-resistant strains of Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Staphylococcus aureus. Compounds 1 and 3-5 exhibited moderate antibacterial activity, with compound 1 displaying the broadest inhibitory profile. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of integrating metabolomics with bioactivity-guided prioritization for the discovery of antibacterial natural products and further highlight the indispensable role of NMR spectroscopy in the structural elucidation of closely related fungal metabolites.

title: Genome-wide identification and characterization of the PE/PPE gene family in Mycobacterium abscessus
abstract: Mycobacterium abscessus (Mab) is a rapidly growing non-tuberculous mycobacterium that causes opportunistic infections and exhibits extensive intrinsic antibiotic resistance. The proline-glutamate (PE) and proline-proline-glutamate (PPE) protein families are mycobacteria-specific virulence factors implicated in immune modulation, antigenic variation, and persistence. While Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) harbors approximately 170 PE/PPE members, the repertoire of PE/PPE genes in Mab remains largely uncharacterized. Here, we performed a genome-wide survey of PE/PPE genes in Mab ATCC 19,977 and identified 18 candidate family members, representing a relatively small fraction of the genome compared with slow-growing mycobacteria. Most predicted proteins harbor canonical PE or PPE domains and display acidic physicochemical properties. Phylogenetic analysis resolved the proteins into three subfamilies: PE, PPE, and PE-PPE, revealing moderate structural diversity but limited family expansion. Motif and gene structure analyses supported the evolutionary conservation. Notably, no PE_polymorphic GC-rich repetitive sequence (PE_PGRS) or PPE_major polymorphic tandem repeat (PPE_MPTR) members were detected, suggesting lineage-specific genomic reduction relative to other pathogenic mycobacteria. AlphaFold predictions revealed conserved N-terminal folds and variable C-terminal regions, which may contribute to functional diversification. Subcellular localization predictions indicated that most proteins are extracellular. Synteny analysis revealed no detectable collinearity among these genes. Transcriptomic analyses revealed condition-dependent expression of PE/PPE genes during amoeba and macrophage infection and under artificial sputum medium and metal ion stress, suggesting roles in environmental adaptation and host interaction. This study provides the first systematic overview of PE/PPE gene repertoire in Mab and lays the groundwork for elucidating their roles in intracellular survival, host interaction, and antimicrobial resistance.

title: Occurrence, distribution, and risks of antibiotics in mollusks from the coast of South China
abstract: To assess the contamination status and health risks of antibiotics in mollusks from South China, this study investigated the enrichment characteristics of 20 antibiotics in 104 mollusk samples collected from 15 coastal cities. Among the mollusk samples analyzed, Guangdong Province exhibited the highest total antibiotic concentration (Σ20Antibiotics), ranging from 45.70 to 343.9 ng gdry weight (dw), with a mean value of 143.1 ng gdw. β-Lactam and tetracycline antibiotics were identified as the predominant classes. A positive correlation was observed between the trophic level of mollusks and the concentrations of these two antibiotic classes. All trophic magnification factors (TMFs) exceeded 1, indicating potential biomagnification of β-lactam and tetracycline antibiotics within mollusks. Both carcinogenic and non-carcinogenic health risks posed by antibiotic residues in mollusks to consumers were at acceptably low levels. Nevertheless, the dissemination risk of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) resulting from antibiotic pollution remains a persistent potential health threat warranting continued vigilance.

title: Salinity-dependent effects of erythromycin on biofilm development and conjugative plasmid transfer on poly(vinyl chloride) microplastics
abstract: Microplastics (MPs) and antibiotics frequently co-occur in aquatic environments and jointly influence the dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs). However, the modulatory role of salinity, a highly dynamic factor in estuarine and coastal regions, remains underexplored. This study investigated the effects of erythromycin (ERY) on biofilm development and RP4 plasmid conjugative transfer on poly(vinyl chloride) (PVC) MPs across varying salinity levels (5‰, 10‰, and 15‰). Results demonstrated that MP hydrophobicity increased with salinity, while the ERY adsorption capacity followed the order: 5‰ > 15‰ > 10‰. A higher salinity (15‰) promoted biofilm biomass and extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) secretion on MPs. Notably, conjugative transfer frequencies within MP-associated biofilms were consistently higher than those in planktonic cultures. Under varying salinities, the conjugation frequencies in biofilms displayed a U-shaped trend, with higher rates observed at 5‰ and 15‰ compared to 10‰. Crucially, the impact of ERY on plasmid transfer was highly salinity-dependent, i.e., the addition of ERY promoted conjugation at 5‰ and 10‰ but significantly inhibited it at 15‰. Physiological assessments revealed that exposure to varying salinities and ERY induced non-lethal oxidative stress, evidenced by elevated reactive oxygen species and upregulated antioxidant enzymes (CAT and SOD), while lipid peroxidation (MDA) remained relatively low. Concurrently, intracellular proline accumulation and cell membrane permeability increased significantly with rising salinity. These findings provide direct experimental evidence that salinity fluctuations and antibiotic residues jointly alter bacterial physiological states and antibiotic resistance dissemination on MPs, which highlights the necessity of considering dynamic environmental variables in ecological risk assessments.

title: Supercritical CO(2) extraction of onion seed oil and its synergistic effect with gentamicin against bacterial strains
abstract: Antibiotic resistance represents a major global health challenge, requiring innovative strategies to enhance the effectiveness of existing antimicrobial agents. In this study, onion seed oil was extracted using supercritical COand evaluated for its potential to improve the antibacterial activity of the antibiotic gentamicin. The oil was characterized through physicochemical analyses, including FTIR spectroscopy, thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Antibacterial activity was tested againstandusing the disk diffusion method. The results demonstrated that onion seed oil exhibited significant antibacterial activity and enhanced the efficacy of gentamicin when used in combination. The synergistic interaction increased inhibition zone diameters by up to 20.4% forand 22.95% for, even at low extract concentrations. These findings suggest that supercritical CO-extracted onion seed oil may serve as a promising natural adjuvant to improve antibiotic performance and combat bacterial resistance.

title: Stepwise accumulation of SecA mutations enables high-stringency azide-based selection in Escherichia coli
abstract: The global spread of multidrug-resistant bacteria has reduced the effectiveness of many conventional antibiotics and complicated genetic analyses that rely on antibiotic resistance genes as selection markers. Genetic selection systems that do not rely on antibiotic-resistance genes are therefore increasingly important, particularly for multidrug-resistant strains. Sodium azide (Az) inhibits the essential ATPase SecA, but previously reported secA mutations confer only limited resistance and have not been developed into practical plasmid-based markers; plasmid-borne secA (F598L) confers only marginal resistance in an Az-sensitive background. Here, we show that this limited resistance results from coexistence of plasmid-derived mutant SecA with chromosomal wild-type SecA, which attenuates the resistant phenotype. The combination of F598L with a newly identified G516C mutation markedly enhanced Az resistance. Chromosomal replacement with secA (G516C/F598L) confirmed that wild-type SecA suppresses the resistant phenotype when coexpressed. Using error-prone PCR, we further generated cumulative SecA mutants and identified a variant harboring five amino acid substitutions (G516C, F598L, L279P, S678I, and A867G) that supported substantially improved, though progressively reduced, growth in liquid culture at Az concentrations up to 200 µg ml. Collectively, these results demonstrate that cumulative SecA mutations can overcome Az-mediated inhibition and provide a plasmid-borne marker that does not itself encode antibiotic resistance. In the present prototype, stable recovery of transformants still required co-selection with tetracycline, and selection by Az alone remains to be achieved. The system nonetheless represents a proof of concept in E. coli that, given the conserved essentiality of SecA, is conceptually extendable to other bacteria, including multidrug-resistant strains.

title: High-risk antimicrobial resistance genomic traits in multidrug-resistant Salmonella across China's food chain: projections to 2050
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is rising globally, yet factors shaping its genomic evolution remain poorly understood. We investigated how socioeconomic, climate, and health factors are associated with AMR spread in multi-drug resistant (MDR) Salmonella enterica across China's food chain, mapped hotspots and forecasted genomic trait prevalence to 2050. We analysed 2,536 MDR genomes from 15 provinces over 16 years, covering patients, food and non-food workers, meat, livestock, and environmental sources. A machine learning framework integrated genomic surveillance with risk assessment to identify high-risk AMR traits (clinically relevant, MDR, mobile). Regression models linked trait prevalence to socioeconomic, climate, health, and antimicrobial consumption data, informing projections to 2050. Eighty-four high-risk traits, including carbapenem, colistin, and β-lactam resistance, are projected to rise, with antibiotic use, population growth, healthcare spending, and urbanisation. Projections were trait-specific: blaand blamay increase up to 20%, while blaand blaremain below 5%. A mechanistic shift in fluoroquinolone resistance is projected: mutation-based resistance (gyrA 87) declines while plasmid-mediated genes (qnrB17, qnrS1) rise. Food workers emerged as a potential reservoir, showing higher trait prevalence than food sources, uniquely carrying last-resort antibiotic-resistance genes (bla, bla, bla). Integrating genomic with socioeconomic surveillance could shift AMR interventions from reactive to preventive.

title: Pooled prevalence of third-generation cephalosporin resistance among Escherichia coli bloodstream isolates in Southeast Asia: protocol for systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Bloodstream infections remain a major contributor to global infectious disease mortality, and antimicrobial resistance increasingly compromises effective empirical and definitive treatment.is among the leading bacterial causes of bloodstream infections and a major pathogen associated with antimicrobial resistance-related mortality. Resistance to third-generation cephalosporins, including ceftriaxone, cefotaxime and ceftazidime, is clinically important because it may limit standard treatment options and increase reliance on broader-spectrum agents. In Southeast Asia, available data on third-generation cephalosporin-resistantbloodstream isolates remain fragmented across countries, hospitals, populations and study designs. This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to estimate the pooled prevalence of third-generation cephalosporin resistance (3GCR) amongbloodstream isolates in Southeast Asia. This protocol will follow the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Protocols (PRISMA-P) guideline and has been registered in PROSPERO under registration number CRD420261381302. Searches will be conducted in PubMed, Scopus, ScienceDirect and Google Scholar from database inception to 1 October 2026, supplemented by citation searching and reference list screening. Eligible studies will include cross-sectional, surveillance, cohort, retrospective laboratory database and prospective observational studies conducted in Southeast Asian countries that report blood culture-specific data on third-generation cephalosporin resistance amongisolates. Studies reporting ceftriaxone, cefotaxime or ceftazidime resistance, or ESBL phenotype clearly representing third-generation cephalosporin resistance, will be considered. Title and abstract screening will be performed independently by three reviewers. Full-text assessment, data extraction and quality assessment will be performed independently by two reviewers, with disagreements resolved through discussion with a third reviewer. Methodological quality will be assessed using a modified version of the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. The primary outcome will be the pooled prevalence of third-generation cephalosporin resistance amongbloodstream isolates. A random-effects meta-analysis will be used, with planned subgroup analyses by country, age group and infection-acquisition setting. Temporal trends will be explored using the year of data collection or publication. Ethical approval is not required because this study will synthesise data from previously published studies and will not involve direct recruitment of human participants or collection of individual patient data. The findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications and conference presentations. CRD420261381302.

title: Genomic epidemiology of Salmonella from retail chicken meat in Japan: decline in pESI-like plasmid-harboring S. Infantis ST32 and predominance of S. Schwarzengrund ST241
abstract: Salmonella is a major foodborne pathogen, and chicken meat is an important source of infection. This study investigated Salmonella prevalence, serovar distribution, antimicrobial resistance, and genomic characteristics in 150 retail chicken meat samples collected in Japan in 2023. The predominant serovar was S. Schwarzengrund (42.7%), followed by S. Infantis (7.3%), which has long been the predominant serovar in Japan. The globally expanding S. Infantis sequence type (ST) 32 harboring pESI-like plasmids has declined in Japan. In contrast, S. Schwarzengrund ST241 was isolated more frequently in winter (66%) than in summer (31%, P < 0.001) and more often from chicken meat produced in eastern Japan (47.1%) than in western Japan (29.4%, P = 0.042). Antimicrobial resistance was most common to tetracycline (50.6%) and streptomycin (45.7%), whereas kanamycin resistance (33.3%) had declined compared with 2015 to 2019, consistent with reduced use of this antimicrobial in broiler production. Moreover, the proportion of S. Schwarzengrund isolates lacking antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) increased markedly from summer (19.4%) to winter (45.5%). cgMLST analysis revealed that antimicrobial-susceptible S. Schwarzengrund isolates formed the largest clade and, notably, retained pESI-like plasmids despite apparent loss of ARG-containing regions from these plasmids. These findings demonstrate ongoing genomic shifts in Salmonella populations in Japan and underscore the need for continuous genomic surveillance to mitigate their public health impact.

title: Appropriate administration of tazobactam/piperacillin for urinary and genital tract infections based on antibiotic susceptibility testing: a single-center retrospective analysis
abstract: Tazobactam/piperacillin (TAZ/PIPC) is a broad-spectrum antimicrobial agent. However, improper administration may contribute to antimicrobial resistance (AMR). The objectives of this study were to evaluate the appropriateness of TAZ/PIPC administration for UGTI based on antibiotic susceptibility testing and to elucidate the patients for whom alternative antibiotics can be utilized as the initial empiric therapy. Patients diagnosed with UGTI at the University of Toyama Hospital between January 2022 and December 2024 who received TAZ/PIPC as initial empirical therapy were analyzed retrospectively. The appropriateness of alternative agents was determined by assessing bacterial culture and antimicrobial susceptibility results. Sixty-two UGTI episodes were analyzed. TAZ/PIPC utilization appeared appropriate in 91.9% of cases. Enterococcus faecalis and Pseudomonas aeruginosa were isolated more frequently in UGTI with devices or ileal urinary diversions compared to UGTI without devices. For patients with ileal urinary diversions or devices, the differences in the appropriateness rates of TAZ/PIPC versus CFPM, CTRX, and SBT/ABPC were higher than those for patients without devices. In patients without devices, the appropriateness rates of TAZ/PIPC, CFPM, CTRX, and SBT/ABPC were 96.7% (29/30), 86.7% (26/30), 83.3% (25/30), and 80.0% (24/30), respectively. Multivariate logistic regression analysis revealed that only the presence of an ileal urinary diversion, a urethral catheter, or a ureteral stent was a risk factor for the inappropriateness (p < 0.05) for CFPM, CTRX, and SBT/ABPC. Based on antibiotic susceptibility testing, TAZ/PIPC may be considered for UGTI using devices or ileal urinary diversions. However, alternative antibiotics may be considered for UGTIs without indwelling devices.

title: Delivery and adherence of biomarker-guided antibiotic treatment protocols in the ADAPT-Sepsis clinical trial: an in-trial descriptive process evaluation of daily procalcitonin- and C-reactive protein-guided protocols
abstract: Biomarker-guided antibiotic protocols using daily procalcitonin or C-reactive protein have been proposed to optimise antibiotic duration in sepsis. This pre-planned process evaluation of the ADAPT-Sepsis trial examined delivery and clinician adherence to procalcitonin- and C-reactive protein-guided protocols. An embedded descriptive process evaluation was conducted within the multicentre ADAPT-Sepsis trial including 2760 adults across 41 UK critical care units. Patients were assigned to procalcitonin-guided, C-reactive protein-guided or standard care. Algorithm-generated recommendations (strong stop, suggest stop or standard care) were relayed to research staff and clinicians who remained blinded to group allocation. Adherence was defined as stopping biomarker sampling after advice. Advice timings, frequencies, adherence rates and reasons for non-adherence were recorded and analysed. Among 2760 patients, strong stop advice occurred earlier in those allocated to the procalcitonin-guided group compared with the C-reactive protein-guided group (mean difference -1.7 days, 95%CI -2.5 to -0.9, p < 0.001). C-reactive protein guidance generated a higher proportion of standard care advice (mean difference -9.1%, 95%CI -10.9% to -7.3%, p < 0.001). Overall advice adherence was greater in patients allocated to the C-reactive protein group than those allocated to the procalcitonin group (mean difference -6.8%, 95%CI -9.0 to -4.5, p < 0.001), driven by the higher proportion of standard care advice and later stronger stop advice with higher adherence (mean difference -14.3%, 95%CI -21.8 to -6.8, p < 0.001). Reasons for advice non-adherence included fixed-duration microbiology guidance, illness severity, continuing fever and elevation of routine inflammatory markers, which did not differ between groups. A C-reactive protein-guided discontinuation protocol achieved higher clinician adherence, probably because its recommendations aligned more closely with established prescribing norms. In contrast, procalcitonin guidance produced earlier and more frequent stop signals, offering greater potential to reduce antibiotic exposure but requiring clinicians to accept earlier discontinuation than usual practice.

title: Application of machine learning to identify risk factors for bloodstream infections caused by different antimicrobial resistance phenotypes in chemotherapy patients
abstract: Bloodstream infections (BSIs) remain a major cause of morbidity and mortality in patients undergoing chemotherapy. The rising incidence of multidrug-resistant organisms (MDROs) further challenges the adequacy of empirical antimicrobial therapy. Therefore, this study aimed to identify features associated with different microbiological profiles of BSIs in chemotherapy patients using machine learning models. We retrospectively analyzed 1435 confirmed BSI episodes among 1220 patients treated at a tertiary cancer center from 2017 to 2022. A multi-label classification approach was used to model BSIs associated with carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative bacilli (CR-GNB), methicillin-resistant staphylococci, third-generation cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales (3GCRE), fungal pathogens, and non-MDRO/non-fungal. Classifier chain models based on logistic regression, random forests, neural networks, and gradient boosting were trained and evaluated using cross-validation with an independent test set. Model outputs were interpreted using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to estimate feature contributions. Most BSIs occurred during the first chemotherapy cycle and were due to non-MDROs or fungal agents (1193 episodes; 83.1%), CR-GNB was identified in 109 (7.6%). Model performance varied across pathogen groups, with the highest discrimination observed for CR-GNB (AUC-ROC 83.25%; 95% CI 73.91%-91.64%). Key features included hospitalization days, hematologic malignancy, prior MDRO infection, monocytopenia, and palliative chemotherapy. Chemotherapy class contributed differently across pathogen groups, with alkylating agents contributing to candidemia, antitumor antibiotics to CR-GNB, and antimetabolites to 3GCRE. Prior CR-GNB infection was the strongest predictor for CR-GNB BSI, while palliative chemotherapy correlated with non-MDRO/non-fungal BSI. Multi-label machine learning approaches may help disentangle the complex etiologies of BSIs in cancer patients by identifying associations between host factors, prior MDRO infection, and chemotherapy class within confirmed BSI episodes, informing future hypothesis generation.

title: Local temperature and humidity are associated with proportion of antimicrobial-resistant Escherichia coli isolates in farm environments: considerations for on-farm surveillance
abstract: Evidence suggests that increased local temperatures are associated with higher prevalence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in environmental bacteria. This observational cohort study investigates associations between local climate and the proportion of antimicrobial-resistantisolated from 2,766 farm environment samples from 53 English dairy farms. A non-linear Bayesian model that accounts for decreased test sensitivity at lowabundance was used to estimate the proportion of antimicrobial-resistantfrom colony count data. A 20°C increase in local temperature was associated with a 5.0-fold increase in the proportion of streptomycin-resistant(95% credible interval [CI]: 1.03-33.0; absolute increase: 0.2%, 95% CI: 2.3 × 10%-1.2%). Weaker evidence suggested that increased temperatures were associated with increased proportions of tetracycline-resistant. Increasing relative humidity was associated with an increase in the proportion of amoxicillin-, streptomycin-, and tetracycline-resistant. A 32% increase in relative humidity (from 60% to 92%) was associated with a 4.7-fold increase in the proportion of amoxicillin-resistant(median; 95% CI: 1.4-15.7; absolute increase: 1.3%, 95% CI: 0.2%-3.5%). For amoxicillin and streptomycin, a synergistic effect where increasing both temperature and humidity was associated with increased proportions of antimicrobial-resistantwas observed, with weak evidence of this effect observed for tetracycline. These findings highlight the importance of considering weather conditions, sample characteristics, and seasonality in livestock AMR surveillance. Associations between local weather conditions and the proportion of livestockexhibiting AMR suggest that climate change may influence the burden of One Health AMR.IMPORTANCEUnderstanding how environmental conditions are associated with variability in antimicrobial resistance (AMR) prevalence is critical for developing robust livestock AMR surveillance and anticipating the potential effects of climate change. The non-linear Bayesian modeling approach developed here adjusts forabundance-associated variability in test sensitivity, enabling the influence of risk factors associated with the proportion of antimicrobial-resistantwithin samples to be more accurately estimated. Applying this approach to 2,766 fecal samples from 53 dairy farms in Southwest England indicated that the proportion of antimicrobial-resistantgenerally increased under warmer and wetter conditions. These findings suggest that environmental conditions can influence the prevalence of antimicrobial-resistantin dairy farm environments and demonstrate the importance of accounting for weather-related variability in livestock AMR surveillance. Adjusting for these associations in livestock AMR surveillance could improve the accuracy of modeling AMR trends and strengthen the assessment of climate-associated AMR risks.

title: Combined Residues of Frequently Detected Herbicides are Stronger Predictors of Soil Resistome and Virulence Potential than Single Residues
abstract: Overuse of herbicides has resulted in a global epidemic of evolved resistance in soil ecosystems. While single herbicide risk has been documented, the impact of multiple herbicide residues on the soil resistomes remains poorly understood. Our study quantified the residues of 24 herbicides, profiled antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) and virulence factor genes (VFGs), and reconstructed 1086 metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) from 93 agricultural soils across China. The analytical results demonstrate that the frequently detected herbicide residues (e.g., 60-90% detection frequency) are stronger predictors of soil antibiotic resistomes than total herbicide load, unsupervised mixture based on principal component analysis (PCA), or single-herbicide models. For VFG abundance, the same mixture outperformed the best single herbicide and total herbicide concentration, although PCA-PC1 showed a moderately stronger correlation. Specifically, these commonly detected herbicides showed positive associations with ARG abundance through both direct linkages and bacterial community-dependent indirect pathways. Similar patterns were observed for virulence potential, where frequently detected residues maintained strong predictive performance and were predominantly associated with indirect pathways. Functional annotation patterns further suggest a concurrent enrichment of traits related to antioxidant defense, mobility, adherence, and immune modulation under elevated herbicide exposure. Notably, multiple herbicide residues were linked to the abundance of a Trinickia taxon, which was identified as a candidate ARG-VFG co-occurrence MAG carrying a high ARG load. Our findings highlight the need to integrate compound exposure of frequently detected herbicides into future risk assessment methodology for preventing the dissemination of ARGs in agricultural soils.

title: Niche Divergence-Based Identification of Microbial Indicators Tracking Cyanobacterial Bloom Succession: A Metagenomic and Machine Learning Framework
abstract: Cyanobacterial harmful algal blooms (CyanoHABs) pose significant environmental and public health risks through toxin production, antibiotic resistance gene dissemination, and the disruption of biogeochemical cycles. Although extensive metagenomic investigations have explored microbial interactions between Cyanobacteria and coexisting members, the potential of incorporating functional indicators into early CyanoHAB monitoring systems remains underexplored. In this study, we employed metagenomic binning combined with machine learning approaches to analyze seasonal cyanobacterial succession and coexisting microbial communities across 19 sites in Erhai Lake across four seasons. We documented distinct niche shifts driven by the spatiotemporal heterogeneity in seasonal cyanobacterial succession alongside the formation of unique niches triggered by this asynchrony. Specialized microbial members (SN-MAGs) were identified as candidate bioindicators associated with early-stage cyanobacterial proliferation. Functional profiling showed r/K selection and metabolic adaptations in these SN-MAGs, including stress resistance and altered carbon metabolism, linked to cyanobacterial dynamics. Machine learning models leveraging these features were constructed and retrospectively evaluated. Cross-lake validation using an independent Lake Taihu dataset confirmed associations among these features and microbial community shifts preceding Microcystis proliferation. Our findings highlight the potential value of the dynamics of specific bacteria as a sensitive indicator of cyanobacterial dynamics. Moreover, we propose that these identified functional markers could potentially be developed into targeted molecular assays (e.g., qPCR assays), offering possible utility in predicting Microcystis population expansion.

title: Challenging the norm: are cefixime challenges relevant in confirmed penicillin-allergic patients?
abstract: Growing evidence suggests that cross-reactivity between penicillins and cephalosporins is mainly driven by R1 side-chain similarity rather than the beta-lactam core. Although cefuroxime, ceftriaxone and cefixime appear to have a low cross-reactivity risk, their use in patients with confirmed penicillin hypersensitivity (HS) remains inconsistent. We aimed to assess the prevalence of HS to cephalosporins with structurally distinct R1 side chains in patients with penicillin allergy.A retrospective analysis of patients who completed allergy workup between 2010 and 2024 at a tertiary center was conducted. Patients with confirmed penicillin HS - established by positive specific IgE, basophil activation test, lymphocyte transformation test, positive skin tests (ST), positive drug provocation tests (DPT), and/or reproducible severe reactions - were included. Patients underwent ceftriaxone ST and cefixime or cefuroxime DPT to assess tolerance to an alternative beta-lactam.Among 241 patients with confirmed penicillin HS, 214 (88.8%) underwent alternative DPT with cefixime (n = 210) or cefuroxime (n = 4). One patient (0.4%) had a positive intradermal ST to ceftriaxone and was not challenged with the alternative cephalosporin. Two patients (0.9%) developed HS reactions during cefixime DPT. Overall, 98.8% of patients tolerated the selected cephalosporins (95% CI 96.3-99.7). A pediatric subgroup was included (n = 40, 16.6%), and no child reacted to the alternative cephalosporins.In this 14-year real-life cohort, 98.8% of the patients with confirmed penicillin HS tolerated a cephalosporin with a structurally distinct R1 side chain, supporting its' safe use in those cases and suggesting that routine hospital-based alternative DPT may be unnecessary in selected patients.

title: Live biotherapeutics in the post-antibiotic era: exploring the potential of probiotics to counter multidrug resistance
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major global health threat that compromises the effectiveness of existing antibiotics and highlights the urgent need for alternative and adjunctive therapeutic strategies. Probiotics have emerged as potential adjunctive strategies because of their ability to modulate host-microbe interactions and influence microbial ecology without promoting resistance. This review examines the current evidence on the potential role of probiotics in combating multidrug-resistant organisms, based on findings fromstudies, animal models, and clinical investigations. The review is based on a narrative literature search of the PubMed database, covering studies published between 2020 and 2025, with earlier landmark studies. The mechanisms discussed include competitive exclusion of pathogens, the production of antimicrobial compounds, the enhancement of intestinal barrier function, and the modulation of host immune responses. In addition, probiotics are evaluated for their capacity to interfere with quorum sensing and inhibit biofilm formation, thereby reducing pathogen virulence and colonization. The review also addresses key limitations, including strain-specific variability, safety concerns in vulnerable populations, and the lack of standardized clinical protocols. Current evidence suggests that probiotics may represent a useful adjunct to existing AMR management strategies. However, their broader clinical application requires larger research to establish their efficacy and safety.

title: An in Silico Characterisation of ATP-Binding Cassette Transporter Proteins Across Five Endodontic Pathogens: Implications for Antimicrobial Resistance and Virulence
abstract: ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter proteins play pivotal roles in antimicrobial resistance and bacterial virulence. However, their characterisation across major endodontic pathogens remains limited. This study aimed to characterise ABC transporter proteins in silico across five endodontic pathogens and to investigate their implications for antimicrobial resistance and virulence. Reference genome-predicted proteomes of Enterococcus faecalis, Porphyromonas gingivalis, Fusobacterium nucleatum, Actinomyces naeslundii and Dialister invisus were retrieved from the National Center for Biotechnology Information RefSeq database. ABC transporter proteins were identified using InterProScan and HMMER and assigned to five functional categories based on Pfam domain signatures. Physicochemical parameters were computed and analysed by principal component analysis, the Kruskal-Wallis test and the chi-square test of independence. Domain architecture and phylogenetic analyses were performed using MAFFT, FastTree and Interactive Tree of Life. A total of 574 ABC transporter proteins were identified (range: 63-168 per species), with A. naeslundii exhibiting the highest transporter density (55.3 per Mb). Putative multidrug resistance pumps were dominant (78.7%) and were highest in F. nucleatum (87.1%) and E. faecalis (82.2%). Functional category distribution differed significantly between species (χ = 22.043, df = 8, p = 0.005). Significant inter-species differences were identified in Grand Average of Hydropathy (GRAVY) score, aromaticity, isoelectric point and instability index (all p < 0.001). BLASTP confirmed the efrAB efflux operon in E. faecalis (EfrA: 99.65%; EfrB: 100.00%) alongside 13 homologue proteins. The dominance of putative multidrug resistance pumps, including sequence-confirmed efrAB proteins and 13 homologues in E. faecalis, provides a plausible molecular framework for intrinsic resistance to intracanal medicaments in persistent endodontic infections.

title: Australian Gonococcal Surveillance Program, 1 January to 31 March 2026
abstract: The Australian National Neisseria Network (NNN) comprises reference laboratories in each state and territory that report data on antimicrobial susceptibility testing to an agreed group of antimicrobial agents for the Australian Gonococcal Surveillance Programme (AGSP). The AGSP data are presented quarterly in tabulated form, as well as in the AGSP annual report. This report presents national gonococcal antimicrobial resistance surveillance data from 1 January to 31 March 2026.

title: Australian Gonococcal Surveillance Programme Annual Report, 2025
abstract: The Australian Gonococcal Surveillance Programme (AGSP) has continuously monitored antimicrobial resistance in(NG) for more than 45 years through the system of jurisdictionalreference laboratories, the National Neisseria Network (NNN). In 2025, a total of 10,204 isolates across Australia, from public and private sectors, were tested for in vitro antimicrobial susceptibility by standardised methods. In 2025, the AGSP captured antimicrobial susceptibility data for 23.9% of all gonococcal infection notifications nationally. The current treatment recommendation for gonorrhoea, for the majority of Australia, continues to be dual therapy with ceftriaxone and azithromycin. In 2025, of NG isolates tested, 0.73% (74/10,204) met the World Health Organization (WHO) criterion for decreased susceptibility (DS) to ceftriaxone, defined as a minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) ≥ 0.125 mg/L. This proportion of isolates meeting the ceftriaxone DS criterion was greater than that reported in 2024 (0.51%), with the majority from New South Wales and Victoria. Genomic analysis indicated that 64.9% of these isolates (48/74) possessed the mosaic penA 60.001 allele, the key target associated with ceftriaxone resistance. Resistance to azithromycin was reported in 7.1% of NG isolates nationally, increasing from being proportionally stable (3.9% to 4.7%) since 2019. Of NG isolates tested, 0.20% (20/10,204) exhibited high-level resistance to azithromycin (MIC value ≥ 256 mg/L), with cases reported across Australia, predominantly in New South Wales, Victoria and non-remote Western Australia. There were ten isolates detected in 2025 that had an extensively drug-resistant (XDR) phenotype: i.e., displaying both high-level resistance to azithromycin and decreased susceptibility to ceftriaxone (MIC ≥ 0.125 mg/L). When added to the 14 XDR isolates reported during 2022-2024, this brings the total to 24 XDR NG isolates reported in Australia since 2022. Genomic analyses of the ten XDR isolates reported in 2025 indicated all harboured the mosaic penA 60.001 allele, with several differing sequence types (ST) identified. By contrast, during 2022 and 2024, XDR NG sequence types were limited to ST-16406, consistent with reports from Europe and England. Travel information, where available, indicates infections in 2025 were associated with travel to Southeast Asia but also arose where no travel was involved. In 2025, penicillin resistance was found in 23.4% of gonococcal isolates, and ciprofloxacin resistance in 59.3% of isolates where tested, although there was variation by jurisdiction particularly in remote settings, where acquisition of cultures for antimicrobial susceptibility testing is low. Tetracycline resistance has been included in surveillance in the AGSP in recent years, coincident with increasing use of doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis for syphilis and chlamydia. Nationally 36.2% of NG isolates in 2025 were tetracycline resistant, with variation by jurisdiction. No isolates were resistant to spectinomycin; data for gentamicin, whilst no breakpoints are defined, are reported by the AGSP as these data are reportable to the WHO Global Antimicrobial Resistance and Use Surveillance System (GLASS). The emergence of antimicrobial resistant NG in Australia has largely occurred through importation, spread and local transmission. In 2025, in Australia and overseas, increased detection of drug-resistant NG isolates is of significant concern as the threat for the future of the current recommended therapeutic agents is increasingly evident, and no ideal alternate therapeutic agent has been identified. Disease prevention strategies under investigation for the future have included the MenB-4C vaccine, designed to protect against meningococcal disease. Despite early promise, recent results from a large Australian trial indicate the MenB-4C vaccine is not effective at preventing gonorrhoea in men who are at high risk of infection. The AGSP continues to monitor antimicrobial resistance and to identify emerging resistant clones by enhanced surveillance approaches, to inform strategies for disease management and treatment of gonorrhoea in Australia.

title: What are people saying about DoxyPEP? A topic-based analysis of Reddit discussions
Concentration-dependent impacts of ofloxacin on the mobilization-immobilization dynamics of geogenic arsenic in groundwater environment
abstract: Arsenic (As) behaviors in aquifers can be altered by exogenetic antibiotics and antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), which modifies evolution of originally geogenic As-contaminated groundwater while increasing environmental risk of ARGs. The roles of introduced antibiotics in As biogeochemical cycle in groundwater environments however remain elusive mechanistically. Using Shewanella oneidensis (S. oneidensis) as a model, this research elucidates the impacts of varying levels of antibiotic (e.g., ofloxacin) exposure on As fate during microbially-mediated reductive dissolution of host goethite. Under low-level ofloxacin exposure (≤1 μg/L), S. oneidensis restored secretion of riboflavin after a short period of stress adaptation. Conversely, high ofloxacin exposure (≥10 μg/L) consistently depleted aqueous riboflavin and weakened mineral-biomolecule interactions, restricting electron transfer and inhibiting goethite bioreduction. Contrasting changes in the abundances of ARGs (e.g., qnrA) and As efflux gene (e.g., arsB) indicate concentration-dependent reorganization of resistance-associated genetic potential under ofloxacin and As co-exposure, while aqueous As(III) accumulated despite declining arsB abundance. Therefore, the molecular mechanism underlying As migration differs depending upon antibiotic exposure levels. These findings provide novel insights into underestimated effects of concomitant antibiotics on As re-mobilization in geogenic contaminated groundwater.

title: Nationwide Survey of Antimicrobial Stewardship in Korean Hospitals: Insights From the Early Stage of the 2024 National Pilot Implementation
abstract: Antimicrobial stewardship programmes (ASPs) are essential for optimising antibiotic use and mitigating antimicrobial resistance. In Korea, antimicrobial consumption exceeds the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development average, and ASP activities remain fragmented, particularly in smaller hospitals. In November 2024, the National Health Insurance Service introduced a pilot reimbursement scheme to support ASPs in hospitals with ≥ 300 beds. This study aimed to provide baseline data to evaluate its impact. A nationwide web-based survey was conducted between January and February 2025 among 297 hospitals with ≥ 300 beds. The questionnaire was designed to allow comparison with the 2020 national survey and to assess the ASP infrastructure, resources, and practices. Of 153 responding hospitals, 71 participated in the pilot programme. Participating hospitals were typically large, university-affiliated, and metropolitan-based; non-participants were smaller, non-teaching, and regional. Participating hospitals employed more infectious disease specialists (2.96 vs. 0.63) and paediatric infectious disease specialists (0.66 vs. 0.12) and allocated more full-time equivalent staff to ASP activities. Participants had stronger institutional support, including financial (46.5% vs. 1.2%) and workforce (52.1% vs. 2.4%) support. Guidelines, interventions, monitoring, and information technology-based decision support systems were more common in participating hospitals, which were all registered with the Korea National Antimicrobial Use Analysis System. Non-participating hospitals frequently lacked guidelines (62%) and interventions (48%). Both groups reported workforce shortages and insufficient incentives as major barriers. The Korean ASP pilot programme strengthened the stewardship infrastructure in participating hospitals, even early on. However, substantial disparities with non-participating hospitals persist, underscoring the need for tailored support for resource-limited institutions.

title: Microfluidic integrated nucleic acid test (MINT) enabled by coupling FEN1-aided RPA with wax-purification and bead-carrier
abstract: To guide timely antibiotic treatment, a tool for quick antimicrobial resistance gene detection is required. Here a Microfluidic Integrated Nucleic Acid Test platform (namely, MINT) was proposed for point-of-care molecular diagnostics. The platform integrates fast nucleic acid extraction based on hybrid wax-phase purification, and DNA amplification based on our newly developed FEN1-aided RPA (FARPA) into a microfluidic chip. The wax-phase stays solid at room temperature, while becomes liquid at >50 °C to allow the wash of inhibitors carried from extraction buffer, thus the chip keeps stable during storage and transportation. The movement of extracted DNA bound with magnetic beads were controlled by a magnet. The beaded DNA was quickly purified during the flow through the wax phase, and the amplification started once the beaded DNA reached to the well for FARPA. The signal from target-positive sample could be readily sensed by a conventional smartphone. The turnaround time is about 40 min from the sample to the result. The platform was validated by detecting the blaKPC-2 resistance gene of Klebsiella pneumoniae (K. pneumoniae) from urine samples with the reliable detection concentration of 500 CFU/mL, achieving 100% agreement for the 29 clinical urine samples (19 positive, 10 negative) with conventional qPCR. It is easy to adapt the MINT to any other pathogen only by designing the corresponding primers and probes for FARPA. It is promising to apply MINT for bed-site antimicrobial resistance screening just after operation.

title: Antibacterial and antibiofilm activities of ZnO-NPs against Streptococcus suis serotype 9 in vitro
abstract: is an important swine pathogen and an emerging zoonotic threat, with serotype 9 (SS9) increasingly recognized as an important pathogenic serotype. Biofilm formation contributes to the persistence, antimicrobial tolerance, and pathogenicity of, yet effective strategies for controlling biofilm-associated infections caused by SS9 remain limited. In this study, we evaluated the antibacterial and antibiofilm activities of zinc oxide nanoparticles (ZnO-NPs) against SS9 and investigated whether their effects were associated with oxidative stress, biofilm formation, and alterations in virulence-associated genes. The minimum inhibitory concentration and minimum biofilm eradication concentration of ZnO-NPs against SS9 were both 49 μg/mL. ZnO-NPs exhibited potent antibacterial and antibiofilm activities, significantly inhibiting biofilm formation and reducing biofilm viability in a dose-dependent manner. Crystal violet staining demonstrated a marked reduction in biofilm biomass, while SEM analysis revealed substantial disruption of bacterial morphology and biofilm architecture following ZnO-NPs treatment. In addition, ZnO-NPs markedly increased intracellular reactive oxygen species levels, indicating the induction of oxidative stress in SS9. ZnO-NPs treatment also reduced the major extracellular matrix components of the biofilm, including extracellular proteins and extracellular DNA. Furthermore, RT-qPCR analysis showed that ZnO-NPs downregulated the expression of biofilm- and virulence-associated genes, including,,, and. Collectively, these findings indicate that ZnO-NPs exert antibacterial and antibiofilm effects against SS9, accompanied by oxidative stress induction, disruption of biofilm architecture and extracellular matrix, and modulation of biofilm- and virulence-associated genes. ZnO-NPs may, therefore, represent a promising candidate for controlling SS9-associated infections.IMPORTANCEserotype 9 (SS9) is an important pathogen associated with disease in pigs and represents a potential zoonotic threat. The increasing prevalence of antimicrobial resistance highlights the need for alternative approaches to control SS9 infections. In this study, zinc oxide nanoparticles (ZnO-NPs) showed antibacterial and antibiofilm activity against SS9, including disruption of established biofilms. These findings provide evidence for further exploring ZnO-NPs as a non-antibiotic strategy for controlling SS9 infections and support future studies evaluating their safety and efficacy in animals.

title: Large-Scale Comparative Genomics of 1,374 Lactiplantibacillus plantarum Genomes Reveals an Open Pan-genome and Strain-Level Variation in Probiotic-Associated and Safety-Related Genomic Features
abstract: Lactiplantibacillus plantarum is widely studied for food fermentation and probiotic applications, but its functional and safety-related characteristics are strongly strain dependent. Large-scale comparative genomics can characterize this diversity and support genome-informed strain prioritization, although genomic evidence alone does not establish probiotic efficacy or safety. A RefSeq genome collection of L. plantarum was subjected to accession-level auditing, exact-sequence dereplication, and predefined genome-quality filtering, yielding 1,374 unique genomes for final analysis. Genome characteristics, pan-genome structure, probiotic-associated annotation proxies, targeted sequence evidence, predefined safety-related genomic markers, isolation-source metadata, and COG functional annotations were evaluated. The final cohort had a mean genome size of 3.286 ± 0.126 Mb and a mean GC content of 44.419 ± 0.168%. Genome size and GC content showed a negative dataset-level association (Pearson's r = - 0.767; R = 0.588). The observed pan-genome comprised 32,500 gene families, including 1,175 core and 31,325 accessory families, and remained non-saturating, with a Heaps' law exponent of γ = 0.289. Probiotic-associated annotation proxies showed heterogeneous prevalence, and targeted sequence analysis demonstrated that annotation nomenclature could substantially influence apparent marker detection. Evidence-supported antibiotic-resistance markers were detected in 46 genomes (3.35%) and mobile-genetic-element-associated markers in 93 (6.77%), whereas ldhD was detected in 1,372 genomes (99.85%). The predefined descriptive concern score assigned 1,236 genomes (90.0%) to the Lowest Genomic Concern category, 136 (9.9%) to the Low category, and two (0.1%) to the Moderate category. Only 1,327 of the 32,500 gene families received a recognized primary COG assignment. The quality-filtered L. plantarum RefSeq collection exhibits an open, accessory-rich pan-genome and substantial strain-level genomic diversity. Annotation-dependent marker detection, uneven database representation, and the limited discrimination of the descriptive concern score emphasize that genome-based screening should be used for candidate prioritization rather than as evidence of probiotic efficacy or definitive safety. Strain-specific phenotypic and application-relevant safety validation remains essential.

title: Molecular Detection Technologies for Helicobacter pylori Antibiotic Resistance: Current Status and Clinical Implications
abstract: Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infects approximately half of the global population and is closely linked to chronic gastritis, peptic ulcers, and gastric cancer. Antibiotic resistance has become a major global health concern with marked regional variations, severely undermining empirical treatment efficacy. Resistance mechanisms primarily involve target gene mutations, efflux pump overexpression, and altered membrane permeability. This review summarizes resistance mechanisms of commonly used antibiotics against H. pylori, along with diagnostic approaches ranging from phenotypic to molecular methods, the latter offering faster and more precise mutation detection, yet limited by high costs and invasive sampling. Treatment has shifted from clarithromycin-based triple therapy to bismuth-containing quadruple and potassium-competitive acid blocker-based regimens. However, susceptibility-guided therapy faces implementation barriers, and empirical regimens remain prevalent. Future directions emphasize affordable multiplex molecular platforms, resistance surveillance networks, artificial intelligence-driven predictive models, and non-antibiotic adjunctive strategies. Integrating molecular diagnostics with antimicrobial stewardship to transition from empirical to precision-based management is critical for improving eradication rates and curbing further resistance spread.

title: Nano-kinetic implant surface mediates osteo-antibacterial synergy through electromagnetic-mechanical coupling
abstract: Periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) is a devastating complication of total joint arthroplasty, mainly caused by bacterial biofilm formation and antibiotic resistance. Traditional static surfaces rely on contact killing-based bactericidal properties and cannot reliably clear mature biofilms. In this study, we fabricate a remote-activated dynamic biomimetic system, namely a movable magnetic topographic surface (MMTS). Here we show that under the exposure of external electromagnetic field (EMF), the anchored Janus nano-heterodimers oscillate periodically to mechanically disrupt bacterial membranes and eradicates biofilms of Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli. This mechanical force can also activates Piezo1 mechanosensitive ion channel in bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs), inducing calcium oscillations, upregulating gene expression of Runx2 and BMP2, and enhancing extracellular matrix mineralization. In vivo, MMTS combined with EMF exposure eliminates local infection and promoted osseointegration. This remote-activated dynamic biomimetic strategy offers a promising multifunctional platform for PJI treatment, and improved implant osteointegration in clinical orthopedics.

title: Knowledge, attitudes and practices towards antibiotic prescription by veterinarians: A systematic review of qualitative studies
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a public health problem with global impacts. Thus, responsible antibiotic use across human and veterinary health sectors must be fostered. Veterinarians play a crucial role in antimicrobial stewardship (AMS), yet their prescribing attitudes are influenced by a complex interplay of factors. This study aimed to collect and synthesize evidence from qualitative studies focusing on the knowledge, attitudes, and practices of veterinarians regarding antibiotic prescription to identify the factors influencing clinical decisions and contribute to AMS strategies. This systematic review followed PRISMA and ENTREQ guidelines, with a protocol registered in PROSPERO (CRD42024529868). On 15 March 2024, the databases Medline/PubMed, EMBASE, Web of Knowledge, and CAB International were searched without time restrictions, and an updated search was conducted on September 11, 2025. Only qualitative and mixed methods studies involving veterinarians working with companion or food-producing animals were included. Critical appraisal was performed using the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist for qualitative research. After search and screening, 28 studies were included, with data mostly being collected through interviews. In total, 34 influencing factors were identified: intrinsic (n = 12) and extrinsic factors (n = 22). Among the intrinsic factors, professional experience, the need to satisfy client's expectations, fear of clinical complications, and fear of losing clients were the most identified. Among the extrinsic factors, client-related (financial resources, expectations, and compliance), antibiotic characteristics, disease prevention, and animal clinical status were identified as main drivers for antibiotic selection and prescribing. Larger-scale mixed methods or longitudinal studies, especially in underrepresented regions, should be encouraged. Strategies under the One Health approach should be effectively implemented to promote the rational use of antibiotics in veterinary medicine, integrating continuing education, easily accessible, practical, and updated regulatory policies and guidelines, animal facilities improvement, and programs that strengthen communication between veterinarians and animal owners.

title: Modern Sample Pretreatment Approaches for β-Lactam Antibiotics in Complex Matrices: Challenges and Innovations
abstract: β-lactam antibiotics, widely used in human and veterinary medicine, can trigger serious public health concerns through misuse-including antimicrobial resistance and drug residues. The detection of β-lactam antibiotics faces three challenges: unstable β-lactam rings prone to hydrolysis, complex metabolism requiring multi-residue analysis, and trace-level concentrations (μg/kg) with severe matrix interference demanding high sensitivity and accuracy. Thus, systematically optimizing sample analytical methods is essential to enhance monitoring programs and ensure food safety. This review offers a comprehensive overview of contemporary pretreatment methodologies, encompassing well-established techniques such as solid-phase extraction and dispersive liquid-liquid microextraction, as well as innovative approaches including solidification floating organic droplet liquid-liquid microextraction and electromembrane extraction. Recent advancements in pretreatment strategies for β-lactam antibiotics are increasingly oriented toward achieving high extraction and purification efficiency, enhancing environmental sustainability, and improving the reusability of extraction materials. By critically evaluating the advantages and limitations of various techniques, this review aims to support progress in detection accuracy and reliability, increase analytical throughput and efficiency, and reduce operational costs.

title: Fleming Fund Implementation in Kenya: What Have We Learned About Strengthening One Health Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance for Decision-making?
abstract: Kenya has moved from fragmented, pilot-based antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance toward a coordinated One Health system, and its experience, pathways of change, and remaining gaps are relevant for other low- and middle-income settings working to operationalize One Health AMR surveillance.
