Here, we report a narrative overview of programmatic learning using 2018 as the pre-Fleming Fund baseline, drawing on national and global surveillance reports, monitoring frameworks from the Quadripartite indicators, qualitative evidence on governance, implementation and policy evolution across the One Health sectors, and Fleming Fund documentation. Since 2018, AMR surveillance expanded from 2 human health sites to 30 human, animal, and environmental sites by 2025. National reports evolved to integrate AMR, antimicrobial consumption, and antimicrobial use data; routine reporting to global platforms matured; and outputs such as dashboards, reports, and policy briefs informing stewardship, Infection Prevention and Control, regulatory action, and policy decisions. External benchmarks showed improvement in AMR-related capacity, with World Health Organization Joint External Evaluation scores moving from limited to demonstrated capacity for surveillance and multisectoral coordination. Kenya's experience suggests that sustainable progress depends on embedding AMR surveillance within government-led governance structures, technical systems, and coordinated partner support, but sustaining gains will require predictable financing and routine data use.

title: Reflections for the Future of AMR Surveillance and AMR Action
abstract: This paper builds on the other papers in this series to present high-level lessons learnt and considerations for the future of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance and its contribution to action on AMR in low- and middle-income countries. Participatory synthesis involved engagement with individuals who had worked within and alongside the Fleming Fund from a range of organizations and geographies, to scope and solidify lessons learnt and future considerations relevant to a wide range of donors, partners, and policy makers or implementors. Contributors were invited to join a Writing Group, which included individuals from academia, clinical sciences, applied public, animal, environment, and food sciences health, as well as senior scientists and administrators from 14 organizations. The synthesis was informed by contributions to 4 virtual workshops and 3 drafts of the manuscript. Authors read and commented on the drafts, several wrote and referenced sections, and all gave substantive feedback with their reactions to the draft conclusions as consensus was built. Over nearly 10 years, the Fleming Fund achieved significant improvements in AMR surveillance. Analysis of the barriers and enablers across settings and systems highlights key lessons for how surveillance is positioned, funded, used, and innovated upon. The success of future AMR surveillance and its sustainability relies on planning within resource constraints for a sharpened system that focuses the scope, frequency, and depth of data to inform action, technical, and architectural developments directions to streamline investment and financing that supports country-led sustainable approaches. Investment in AMR surveillance and broader AMR actions has yielded substantial progress. Expanded domestic public financing, large-scale private sector engagement, or enhanced multilateral support will be needed to ensure recent gains are sustained. Progress will require well-designed, targeted, and cost-effective investments to maintain current capacity while enabling further system strengthening.

title: The Fleming Fund: Key Features of Design and Approach to Strengthening Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance in Low- and Middle-Income Countries
abstract: This paper examines the Fleming Fund as a major long-term investment in strengthening antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance in low- and middle-income countries. Established by the UK Department of Health and Social Care in 2015, the Fund committed up to £498 million to support surveillance capacity across 25 countries in Africa and Asia through a One Health approach spanning human, animal and environmental health. The paper situates the Fleming Fund within wider global concern about AMR and highlights surveillance as essential for stewardship, policy and international coordination. It describes the Fleming Fund's design logic, governance arrangements, grant architecture and evolving strategic priorities, with particular attention to how the program combined laboratory strengthening, workforce development, data systems, quality assurance, sampling pathways and multisectoral coordination to generate credible and usable AMR data. The analysis also examines the Phase 2 shift from an initial emphasis on data generation toward greater attention to data interpretation, dissemination and use in policy and practice. Drawing on program documentation, evaluation evidence and stakeholder perspectives, the paper presents the Fleming Fund as an important case of large-scale surveillance system strengthening in resource-constrained settings. It argues that the Fund offers wider lessons on the time, coordination and institutional embedding required to move from externally supported capacity building toward sustainable national surveillance functions. These lessons are relevant to future AMR investments and to broader debates on global health security, health systems strengthening and One Health implementation.

title: Generating Actionable Data From Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance: Insights From the Fleming Fund's International Experience
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major global health threat, with the greatest burden falling on low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) also challenged with limited surveillance capacity. The UK Government's Fleming Fund was established in 2015 to strengthen AMR surveillance across Africa and Asia through a One Health approach. This paper draws on program experience, country implementation evidence, and published literature to describe how the Fleming Fund operationalized AMR surveillance, assess its contribution to the quantity and quality of surveillance data, identify key implementation challenges, and consider implications for future global surveillance strategies. The Fleming Fund combined investments in laboratory infrastructure, workforce development, quality assurance, data systems, governance, and data use. Across supported countries, these investments enabled substantial growth in routine bacteriology and antimicrobial susceptibility testing, strengthened reference and surveillance laboratory capacity, increased participation in external quality assessment, and expanded reporting to the World Health Organization's Global Antimicrobial Resistance and Use Surveillance System. The program also supported complementary surveillance approaches, including antimicrobial use and consumption data and, in some settings, burden-of-disease and genomic surveillance. Progress, however, has been uneven and remains vulnerable to fragile infrastructure, procurement and supply chain bottlenecks, workforce turnover, fragmented data systems, weak clinical-laboratory interfaces, limited representativeness, and uncertain long-term financing. The Fleming Fund experience shows that strengthening AMR surveillance in LMICs is feasible, but requires sustained, system-wide investment. Future strategies should prioritize integration with clinical care, stronger digital and analytical capacity, broader diagnostic access, and domestic financing to ensure that high-quality AMR data are generated, shared, and translated into action.

title: Antimicrobial Resistance and One Health: Lessons on One Health Governance and Implementation from the Fleming Fund
abstract: This paper reflects upon the experience of the Fleming Fund in designing and implementing One Health antimicrobial resistance (AMR) programs in 25 countries and identifies practical lessons for the design of future One Health programs. The Fleming Fund experience highlights key priorities for implementing One Health effectively within AMR programs-though many of the insights should be applicable to other contexts as well, such as emerging infectious diseases and health security. One Health should be treated as an approach to problem framing and action rather than a program output, with flexibility for national adaptation. Meaningful implementation requires sustained investment beyond human health, particularly in animal and environmental sectors, to avoid symbolic engagement. Surveillance systems should consider both the role of the sector and sector-specific needs, supported by capacity for joint interpretation and use of evidence. The costs of multisectoral coordination should be explicitly resourced and both formal governance mechanisms and informal professional networks recognized as essential for building trust, sustaining collaboration, and translating data into policy-relevant action.

title: Surveillance Data Use Through the Fleming Fund: Informing Action on Antimicrobial Resistance in Low- and Middle-Income Countries
abstract: Drawing on the Fleming Fund's work to strengthen antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance across Africa and Asia during 2018-2026, this article provides one of the first syntheses of AMR surveillance data use in low- and middle-income countries. A participatory synthesis for narrative review was conducted to summarize experience across administrative levels (facility, subnational, national, and regional). Data use was most evident at the facility level, in human health systems where resistance patterns, antimicrobial use, and clinical data increasingly informed antimicrobial stewardship, infection prevention and control, and other quality improvement initiatives. Data use in other sectors required different approaches. At the national level, Fleming Fund investments were associated with revisions of treatment guidelines, updates of essential medicines lists, and regulatory measures, primarily through improved governance and policy communities. Regional platforms supported member country data use at the national level. Subnational data use was undertaken in countries with decentralized health systems. Across levels, data use pathways driven by local priorities helped surveillance inform action. Fleming Fund experience suggests that surveillance is more likely to inform action when data use is built into system design. Continued investment will be needed if AMR surveillance is to improve policy and practice in low- and middle-income countries.

title: Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) Surveillance: Ten Years On
Culture-based detection of clinically relevant carbapenemase genes in Gram-negative bacteria from aquatic environments in western Algeria
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) requires environmental surveillance because aquatic systems can receive resistant bacteria, antimicrobial residues and mobile resistance genes from domestic, agricultural, hospital and industrial sources. This culture-based study investigated culturable Gram-negative bacteria recovered from 12 inland, saline, wetland and coastal aquatic sites in western Algeria between January and April 2023. Bacterial isolates were identified by conventional biochemical methods and 16 S rRNA gene sequencing. Antimicrobial susceptibility was assessed by disk diffusion and selected broth microdilution assays, with colistin interpreted only by minimum inhibitory concentration. Phenotypic screening for extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-like and carbapenemase-associated activity was followed by targeted PCR and Sanger sequencing in selected high-risk isolates. Fifty-four Gram-negative isolates were recovered, including 44 fermenting and 10 non-fermenting isolates. Ten isolates, all fermenting Gram-negative bacteria, fulfilled the multidrug-resistant definition after exclusion of species-related intrinsic resistance. Targeted sequencing confirmed blaOXA-48 in two Escherichia coli isolates and one Cronobacter sakazakii isolate. One Escherichia coli isolate co-harbored blaNDM-1 and blaOXA-48. The colistin-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolate was negative for mcr-1. These findings provide baseline evidence that selected aquatic environments in western Algeria harbor culturable Gram-negative bacteria carrying clinically important carbapenemase genes. The study should be interpreted as targeted culture-based surveillance rather than a quantitative assessment of the aquatic resistome. These data represent the environmental component of AMR surveillance within a One Health framework and do not establish an epidemiological linkage to human or animal reservoirs.

title: Alternative respiratory electron transport pathways drive differential aminoglycoside susceptibility
abstract: Bacterial bioenergetics is increasingly recognized as a central determinant of antibiotic tolerance and resistance. Here, we define how architectural variation within the aerobic electron transport system (ETS) modulates proton motive force (PMF) and governs antibiotic susceptibility. We constructed fourstrains with unbranched respiratory pathways differing in proton-translocation efficiencies. A low-PMF ETS variant exhibited selective tolerance to aminoglycosides, while susceptibility to β-lactams and tetracycline remained unchanged. Using fluorescent gentamicin, we demonstrate that reduced PMF directly limits drug uptake. Interestingly, wild-typewas as susceptible as the high-PMF variant. These results establish respiratory energy transduction as a mechanistic bottleneck for aminoglycoside efficacy and position ETS remodeling as a bioenergetic route to antibiotic tolerance.IMPORTANCEInfectious diseases remain a major global health challenge, and the failure of antibiotics to effectively treat them is compounding the threat. This study shows that the way bacteria produce energy can strongly influence how well certain antibiotics work. By engineering bacteria with different respiratory pathways, we demonstrate that bacteria in a low-energy state became specifically more tolerant to aminoglycoside antibiotics such as gentamicin and tobramycin. Importantly, this tolerance was linked to reduced drug entry into the cell rather than resistance gained due to acquisition of adaptive genetic change. The findings reveal that bacterial energy metabolism is not simply a housekeeping process, but a major factor determining antibiotic effectiveness. This work helps explain why some bacteria survive antibiotic treatment despite lacking resistance mutations and highlights bacterial respiration as a promising target for developing strategies to restore antibiotic sensitivity and combat persistent infections.

title: Protein malnutrition facilitates intestinal colonization with highly resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae through disrupted intestinal microbial metabolism
abstract: Pediatric infections with highly resistant(HR-Kp) disproportionately affect low-income countries where childhood malnutrition is prevalent. Malnutrition is an identified risk factor for infection with HR-Kp and other antimicrobial-resistant Enterobacterales, but the mechanistic underpinnings of this link and independence from other common exposures, like antibiotics, in children are unclear. Using a murine model of pediatric malnutrition, we found that mice fed a protein-deficient diet (PD) were more susceptible to colonization with HR-Kp at a 4-log lower challenge inoculum and developed a 3-log higher intestinal burden in comparison to adequately nourished mice. HR-Kp colonization in PD-fed mice persisted beyond 5 weeks, and colonization was transmitted to diet-matched cage mates. Antibiotic treatment resulted in similar HR-Kp colonization burdens regardless of diet, suggesting that nutrition-dependent colonization risk is driven by altered intestinal microbiota. Despite reduced dietary protein intake, intestinal amino acid content was maintained in PD-fed mice, supporting optimal HR-Kp growth. Furthermore, secondary bile acids, prototypic intestinal microbiota-derived molecules, were reduced in PD-fed mice, demonstrated an inverse correlation with HR-Kp burden, and partially inhibited the growth of HR-Kp. Collectively, these findings reveal a role for dietary protein intake in determining nutrition-dependent colonization resistance to HR-Kp.IMPORTANCEAntimicrobial-resistantare responsible for a growing mortality burden worldwide, with disproportionate rates of infection in low-income countries where childhood malnutrition is prevalent. Several publications have demonstrated high rates of intestinal colonization with antimicrobial-resistantin children admitted with severe malnutrition in sub-Saharan Africa. However, numerous confounding risk factors in malnourished children (antibiotic use, healthcare exposure, and immune dysfunction) make it difficult to assess the direct impact of nutrition oncolonization. In this study, we utilized a novel mouse model of protein malnutrition to demonstrate that dietary protein deficiency renders mice susceptible to a higher burden of intestinal colonization at a lower inoculating dose of. Furthermore, reduced microbiota-derived bile acid metabolites correlate with increased burden of colonization in protein-deficient mice. These results are the first to establish a direct mechanistic link associating dietary protein deficiency, bile acid metabolism, and intestinal colonization with antimicrobial-resistant.

title: Sequencing-based molecular epidemiology of mesophilic Aeromonas in dairy environments and water systems
abstract: This study investigated the prevalence, virulence gene distribution, antimicrobial resistance, and molecular epidemiology of mesophilicspecies from milk, dairy farm environments, and drinking water systems in Kashmir, India.prevalence varied between sample sources, with environmental samples having the highest detection rate (51.96%), followed by water sources (46.60%) and milk (36.15%). Following pasteurization and disinfection, prevalence in milk samples was significantly reduced, demonstrating the efficacy of hygiene measures in minimizing contamination. Higher detection rates were found in environmental sources like soil, cow dung, and milkers' hands, suggesting their role as potential sources of contamination. The Aeromonads exhibited a wide distribution of virulence determinants; species-associated variations were noted for theandgenes, while thegene was ubiquitous among isolates. Virulence gene distribution differed between species, withexhibiting the most varied virulence profiles. Antimicrobial resistance patterns were generally comparable among the mesophilicspecies, and multidrug resistance was detected in 45.8% of the isolates. Analysis of,, andgenes based on sequencing distinguished isolates into species-specific clades, withproviding the highest intra-species resolution, suggesting its utility as an informative marker for molecular epidemiological investigations of. These results show that water systems and dairy environments are significant sources of genetically diverse Aeromonads carrying virulence and antimicrobial resistance determinants.IMPORTANCEspecies are widely distributed in aquatic environments and are increasingly recognized as emerging opportunistic pathogens, yet their role in dairy production systems remains poorly understood. The prevalence and genetic relatedness of mesophilicspp. across milk, dairy farm environments, and drinking water systems remain underexplored. By integrating prevalence data from a large and diverse collection of samples with virulence profiling, antimicrobial resistance characterization, and sequencing-based molecular epidemiology, the present study provides a comprehensive assessment ofpopulations across these interconnected compartments. The findings underscore the importance of hygienic practices during milk production and the need for routine monitoring of environmental and water sources associated with dairy systems. Improved understanding of the genetic diversity and distribution ofcan support more effective surveillance strategies and help mitigate potential risks to food safety and public health.

title: PASTA kinase dimerization in Enterococcus faecalis does not require the extracellular PASTA domains
abstract: The penicillin- and Ser/Thr-kinase-associated (PASTA) kinase family of bacterial signaling proteins encompasses a widely conserved family of transmembrane Ser/Thr kinases defined by the presence of multiple PASTA domains comprising the extracellular module. PASTA kinases are found in nearly all gram-positive bacteria and are activated in response to cell wall stress to control critical physiological processes. A thorough understanding of the mechanisms of PASTA kinase signaling is important not just for greater insight into bacterial physiology but also to target PASTA kinases for therapeutic intervention. However, many fundamental features of the proposed model for signaling by PASTA kinases have not been tested using full-length kinase in cells of its native host under physiological conditions; hence, the mechanisms of PASTA kinase signaling have remained largely obscure. In this work, we tested fundamental features of the proposed model for PASTA kinase signaling using the representative PASTA kinase of, IreK. Through a combination of genetics and biochemistry, we established that IreK participates in self-association to form dimers incells and that the self-associated form of IreK is functionally important for signaling. However, in contrast to the proposed model for PASTA kinase signaling, IreK dimerization does not require the extracellular PASTA module, and moreover, dimerization does not correlate with IreK signaling. Additionally, dimerization of IreK is not sufficient for kinase activation. Thus, regulation of PASTA kinase signalingis more complex than has been proposed.IMPORTANCEMost gram-positive bacteria encode penicillin- and Ser/Thr-kinase-associated (PASTA) kinases that are activated in response to cell wall stress to control critical physiological processes, including cell division and antibiotic resistance, among others. As such, PASTA kinases have been considered potential targets for new antibiotics. A thorough understanding of the mechanisms of PASTA kinase signaling is important for effective therapeutic intervention. However, the prevailing model for signaling by PASTA kinases has not been tested using a full-length kinase in cells of its native host under physiological conditions; hence, the mechanisms of signaling remain obscure. Here, we showed that the PASTA kinase ofparticipates in self-association to form dimers incells and that the self-associated form is functionally important for signaling. However, some features of the prevailing model for PASTA kinase signaling are inconsistent with our results, suggesting that regulation of PASTA kinase signalingis more complex than has been proposed.

title: The growing zoonotic threat of Babesia and Theileria: the urgent case for piroplasm-specific drug pipelines
NTDB: a curated database of natural transformation machinery and regulatory genes in prokaryotes
abstract: Natural transformation, genetically controlled by specialized machinery and regulatory genes, drives evolution and adaptation in prokaryotes. This process facilitates the spread of clinical traits such as antibiotic resistance. The DNA uptake specificity is mediated by conserved motifs found in certain naturally transformable species. Despite its evolutionary and clinical significance, dedicated resources for natural transformation have been lacking. Here, we present the Natural Transformation DataBase (NTDB) (https://bioinfo-mml.sjtu.edu.cn/NTDB/), which compiles information on machinery and regulatory genes associated with natural transformation in prokaryotes. NTDB integrated experimentally validated data on 118 naturally transformable species, 1072 transformation-associated genes, and 10 DNA uptake motifs identified through literature mining. Homology-based search identified 420 600 machinery genes and 246 164 regulatory genes across 12 310 prokaryotic strains, with comprehensive protein annotations. In addition, the distribution and abundance of DNA uptake motifs in Neisseriaceae and Pasteurellaceae species were quantified. Furthermore, NTDB offers online tools to predict natural transformation-associated genes and DNA uptake motifs via an interactive web interface. NTDB intends to facilitate mechanistic studies of natural transformation machinery and competence regulation.

title: Genomic diversity and antimicrobial resistance determinants among publicly available Mycoplasma genitalium genomes: a comparative phylogenomic analysis
abstract: BackgroundAntimicrobial resistance is increasingly challenging the clinical management ofinfections. This study aimed to characterize the genomic diversity, population structure, molecular typing profiles, and distribution of antimicrobial resistance-associated determinants among publicly availablegenomes.MethodsAll 64 genomes publicly available in NCBI and PubMLST at the time of data collection were included. Genomes were characterized byand MG309 molecular typing and screened for mutations associated with macrolide and fluoroquinolone resistance. Phylogenetic relationships were investigated using a recombination-filtered core-genome alignment, and molecular typing and antimicrobial resistance profiles were mapped onto the resulting maximum-likelihood phylogeny.ResultsSubstantial molecular diversity was observed, with 29and 21 MG309 types identified. Macrolide resistance-associated 23S rRNA mutations were detected in 34/64 (53%) genomes. The fluoroquinolone resistance-associated ParC substitutions S83I and S83 R were detected in 14 (22%) and one genome, respectively. Relevant GyrA substitutions were less frequent and occurred exclusively in genomes also carrying ParC S83I. Overall, 15/64 (23%) genomes exhibited a dual-resistance genotype, whereas 19/64 (30%) carried macrolide resistance-associated mutations without concomitant fluoroquinolone resistance markers. Resistance-associated genotypes occurred across multiple phylogenetically distinct genomic backgrounds, while clusters of closely related isolates sharing molecular typing and resistance profiles were also identified. Conventionaland MG309 typing did not consistently recapitulate whole-genome phylogenetic relationships.ConclusionsThese findings reveal substantial genomic diversity and a high frequency of resistance-associated determinants among publicly availablegenomes, supporting the expansion of geographically representative genomic surveillance to monitor the emergence and dissemination of antimicrobial resistance.

title: Production of recombinant human proteins in Komagataella phaffii using a sucrose-utilization-based selection marker without antibiotic resistance
abstract: Komagataella phaffii (K. phaffii) is one of the most widely used eukaryotic expression systems for recombinant protein production. However, its industrial application is constrained by reliance on traditional antibiotic-based selection and the inability to utilize sucrose. Based on the heterologous expression of the sucrose hydrolase SucF from Aspergillus flavus in K. phaffii, the strain acquired the ability to utilize sucrose. It was verified that this trait can serve as a dominant selection marker under sucrose-selective conditions, making SucF a selection marker for antibiotic-free strain construction. Under a selection pressure of 40 g/L sucrose, the gene integration efficiency reached 100 %, comparable to that of traditional antibiotic selection. Notably, this system enables the substitution of the original glycerol carbon source with sucrose for fermentation. To improve the selection efficiency of SucF, a triple mutant (T65A/R322Q/S323G) was identified through computer-aided protein engineering, exhibiting a 57 % increase in sucrose hydrolysis rate compared to the wild type. Structural analysis revealed that this mutation remodels the sucrose-binding pocket. Ultimately, the SucF mutant was used as a selection marker in combination with the histidine auxotrophic marker (HIS4) to achieve secretory expression of human lactoferrin (hLF) and human osteopontin (hOPN) in the GS115, and the resulting recombinant strain was free of antibiotic gene residues. This sucrose-based antibiotic-free platform in K. phaffii provides a promising strategy for green biomanufacturing and industrial production of recombinant proteins devoid of antibiotic resistance genes.

title: Global Distribution and Co-occurrence of Antimicrobial, Biocide, and Metal Resistance Genes in 11,921 Acinetobacter baumannii Genomes
abstract: Acinetobacter baumannii is a critical priority pathogen globally. While antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) are well characterized, the prevalence, distribution, and co-occurrence patterns of biocide and metal resistance genes (BMRGs) remain poorly defined at global scale. We performed genomic analysis of 11,921 non-redundant A. baumannii genomes retrieved from NCBI RefSeq, representing isolates from 93 countries collected between 1982 and 2025. ARGs and BMRGs were identified using AMRFinderPlus (v4.2.7; organism-specific mode). Multilocus sequence typing (Pasteur MLST) was performed, and BMRG-ARG co-occurrence was assessed using one-sided Fisher's exact tests for enrichment with Benjamini-Hochberg correction (q < 0.05). Every genome carried at least one AMR determinant, and 99.98% carried at least one biocide or metal resistance locus at initial annotation. AMRFinderPlus identified 687 resistance-associated loci (633 AMR determinants; 39 biocide and metal resistance loci, of which 38 BMRGs were retained for analysis after exclusion of the core-genome gene nreB; and 15 virulence-associated loci, which were excluded from resistance analyses). Sequence type 2 (ST2) accounted for 56.4% of genomes. The carbapenemase gene blaOXA-23 was detected in 62.6% of genomes, and fluoroquinolone resistance mutations were highly prevalent (gyrA S81L: 84.9%; parC S84L: 77.2%). Co-occurrence analysis identified 38 significant BMRG-ARG associations overall (q < 0.05, OR ≥ 10), with a prominent module linking the integron-associated marker qacEΔ1 to ARGs (e.g., sul1, aadA1); the population-level mercury resistance-tet(A) association was not supported in the phylogeny-based sensitivity analysis. This study provides quantitative evidence for structured BMRG-ARG co-occurrence patterns in A. baumannii, shaped by ST2 dominance. These patterns are consistent with possible linkage and co-selection, although the present data cannot establish physical linkage.

title: Screening of campylobacter by Gram staining and culture confirmation in diarrheal stool: a qualitative study
abstract: Campylobacter is an important cause of diarrhoeal illness in children. As isolation of these fastidious bacteria from stool samples is laborious and expensive, it is not routinely investigated in certain geographical areas. This study aimed to demonstrate the utility of Gram staining as a rapid and cost-effective screening method for the detection of Campylobacter in stool specimens from children with acute diarrhoea. Stool samples from 138 children below 12 years of age at a tertiary care centre were screened by Gram staining for Gram-negative spiral bacilli. Smear-positive samples were subjected to culture on campylobacter selective medium. Isolates were confirmed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) targeting the genus-specific 16S rRNA gene and the mapA and ceuE genes, to Campylobacter jejuni and C.coli respectively. Antibiotic susceptibility testing was performed by the Kirby-Bauer disc diffusion method against erythromycin and ciprofloxacin. Gram-negative spiral bacilli were detected in 15 (10.86%) and 13 were confirmed by culture (positive predictive value of Gram staining: 86.66%). One sample was positive on direct PCR with no growth. Of the isolates, 11 were identified as C. jejuni, one C.coli, and one as non-jejuni/non-coli. All isolates were susceptible to the tested antibiotics. Gram staining of stool is rapid, low-cost and practical screening method for campylobacteriosis. With positive predictive value of 86.66%, it offers a valuable first-line diagnostic tool. C.jejuni is the predominant species in this paediatric population and the absence of antibiotic resistance supports the continued use of erythromycin and ciprofloxacin as first-line therapeutic agents.

title: AlphaFold-driven structure-based drug discovery: Capabilities, benchmarks and limitations for medicinal chemistry
abstract: Structure-based drug discovery (SBDD) has become an indispensable tool of medicinal chemistry due to the possibility of rational drug design based on the three-dimensional structure of the biological target. Nevertheless, the use of SBDD technology has been restricted due to the scarcity of known experimentally solved structures of the proteins that are the targets of drug action, especially those which are difficult to characterize, poorly understood and associated with diseases. Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based protein structure prediction technologies, such as AlphaFold, have substantially expanded structural biology by generating high-confidence predicted structures for a large fraction of the known proteome, although prediction confidence and accuracy vary considerably by target and by region within a target. This review covers the aspects of SBDD approach, traditional methods of protein structure determination and limitations that have restricted the application of this methodology. Additionally, this review addresses the use of AlphaFold models in major drug discovery processes including target identification, binding site prediction, molecular docking, virtual screening, lead optimization and structure-activity relationships (SAR). The possible utilization of AlphaFold in different areas of medicine, including oncology, antimicrobial resistance, neurodegenerative diseases and targeted protein degradation, is mentioned. Moreover, the collaboration of AlphaFold with new computational technologies, such as machine learning, generative artificial intelligence, molecular dynamics and multi-omics analysis, is described. An evidence-graded decision framework specifies when predicted structures are likely to suffice for hit finding, SAR interpretation, selectivity optimization, fragment-based design and degrader design and where quantitative evidence is still lacking. Even though AlphaFold has substantially advanced the field for example, in a prospective screen against the G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) TAAR1, docking to AlphaFold2 models gave a 60% hit rate versus 22% for a homology model and a workflow combining an AlphaFold model with generative chemistry against the kinase CDK20 yielded a compound with an IC50 of 33.4 nM and an approximately eightfold antiproliferative selectivity window between cell lines-problems related to protein flexibility, conformational changes of proteins due to ligands, binding affinity prediction and biological complexity cannot be neglected and predicted structures still require experimental validation before guiding synthesis.

title: Antibiotic enrichment in seawater from solid-phase extraction to molecularly imprinted polymers and covalent organic frameworks
abstract: Antibiotic residues in seawater and the associated antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) pose serious threats to marine ecosystems and human health. Accurate monitoring of antibiotics depends on efficient enrichment, but the high salinity and complex dissolved organic matter in seawater render conventional solid-phase extraction (SPE) susceptible to severe matrix effects and poor selectivity. This review systematically evaluates the limitations of SPE in seawater matrices and examines two emerging high-selectivity materials, molecularly imprinted polymers (MIPs) and covalent organic frameworks (COFs), focusing on their design principles, synthesis strategies and enrichment performance. MIPs achieve high selectivity through template-directed recognition (imprinting factors typically 2-10) but have limited adsorption capacity (20-150 mg/g for conventional MIPs). COFs exhibit excellent adsorption capacity and mass transfer owing to their high specific surface area (>2000 m/g) but lack sufficient selectivity. Their composite, COF@MIPs, synergistically combines both advantages, with reported 2-5-fold higher adsorption capacity and 40-60% shorter equilibrium time in non-seawater matrices; however, seawater validation remains lacking. This review also summarizes offline and online enrichment coupling strategies with chromatography-mass spectrometry, highlighting the integration of high-selectivity materials into online SPE systems. Future directions should focus on optimizing COF@MIP interfacial synthesis, developing salt-tolerant and antifouling stimuli-responsive materials, integrating them into online SPE systems and standardizing methods, thereby providing key technical support for global marine environmental health monitoring and antibiotic pollution control.

title: Phage preferential infection of antibiotic-susceptible bacteria enriches antibiotic-resistant bacteria in activated sludge microbiomes
abstract: Despite the significance of phages in microbial ecosystems, the contribution of lytic phages to the propagation of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) within activated sludge microbiomes remains unclear. By integrating global metadata analysis and metagenomics, we first demonstrated that lytic phages exhibit a strong infection preference for antibiotic-susceptible bacteria (ASB, 70.84%) over antibiotic-resistant bacteria (ARB, 29.16%). This preferential phage infection was consistent with ARB carrying an exceptionally higher abundance of antiviral defense systems than ASB (averaging 1.83 versus 0.03 systems per whole genome). Furthermore, phage transplant experiments revealed that elevated phage predation pressure (phage-to-bacteria ratios ≥100) drove significant shifts in community composition toward highly defended lineages, thereby enriching the relative abundance of ARGs and mobile genetic elements (MGEs) by 25∼30-fold compared to controls. Additionally, real-time microfluidic tracking confirmed a "Kill-the-Winner" ecological dynamic, where phages selectively eradicate fast-growing ASB, thereby indirectly promoting ARB survival and increasing ARG transfer frequency. Overall, these findings highlight an underappreciated ecological risk driven by selective predation of lytic phages, which indirectly accelerates ARG dissemination in complex environmental microbiomes.

abstract: Glacial forelands in Maritime Antarctica are rapidly expanding due to deglaciation, thereby increasing ecological connectivity among previously isolated microbial reservoirs. From a One Health perspective, this process is relevant because environmental microorganisms represent long-standing reservoirs of antibiotic resistance and virulence-associated traits. However, current knowledge is mainly limited to dominant, fast-growing taxa recovered by conventional cultivation, leaving the functional potential of slow-growing and rare Antarctic bacteria largely unexplored. Here, we compared traditional plating methods (PM) andcultivation (ISC) for recovering bacteria from permafrost, moraine, and rhizosphere soils, quantified total culturable diversity using 16S rRNA metabarcoding, and assessed antibiotic susceptibility and phenotypic virulence across 158 nonredundant isolates. Cultured communities were dominated by Pseudomonadota, Actinomycetota, Bacteroidota, and Bacillota, withamong the most prevalent genera, although its relative abundance varied across soil compartments and cultivation strategies. ISC expanded the taxonomic breadth of cultured bacteria and enabled the recovery of rare or underrepresented genera absent from PM collections, including,,,,,, and. Functional profiling revealed a widespread environmental resistome, with high frequencies of resistance to β-lactams, cephalosporins, and oxazolidinones. Notably, isolates affiliated with,,, andexhibited extreme multidrug resistance, with individual strains resistant to more than 20 antibiotics. Virulence-associated phenotypes were broadly distributed across cultured taxa, including lecithinase and hemolytic activity (>35% of isolates), pyocyanin production (∼20%), and DNase activity (∼7%). Together, these results demonstrate thatcultivation provides access to underrepresented components of Antarctic microbial diversity and reveals resistance- and virulence-associated traits beyond those of dominant taxa. Antarctic glacier foreland soils, therefore, represent underexplored environmental reservoirs of health-relevant microbial functions, underscoring the value of culturomics for environmental health research amid climate-driven change.
